title: Enhancement: Parallelize independent update phases (pip + npm + scoop + dotnet + vscode)
description:
## Finding
pip (line ~890), npm (~899), scoop (~1085), dotnet tools (~1111), and vscode extensions (~1141) are completely independent — none of them install dependencies the others need, none share package locks. Today they run strict-sequentially inside the main loop. Estimated wall-clock savings: ~30-40% of total cycle time on systems with moderate activity in these ecosystems.

## Suggestion
Detect which of these phases are enabled, launch them as background jobs in parallel (or `ForEach-Object -Parallel`), collect results into the per-phase `@{ Success; Count }` shape, and update state atomically. Office365 / Winget / Choco / WindowsUpdate stay sequential because of installer-locking concerns.

## Estimated savings
~30-40% of cycle wall-clock on developer machines.
close_reason: Implemented in Phase C commit

title: Enhancement: BitLocker suspend/resume around forced reboots
description:
## Finding
When the orchestrator reboots a BitLocker-protected system, the next boot may land at the BitLocker recovery prompt rather than the Windows login screen, breaking the unattended loop. This is a hard stall, not merely an inconvenience — the loop hangs until a human types the recovery key.

## Suggestion
Before `shutdown.exe /r`, run `Get-BitLockerVolume | Where-Object { $_.ProtectionStatus -eq "On" } | Suspend-BitLocker -RebootCount 1`. Log a warning if the cmdlet fails (Win11 24H2 has a known bug); fall back to `manage-bde.exe -protectors -disable C: -rebootcount 1`.

## Peer reference
Boxstarter does this universally; it is one of the headline reasons Boxstarter exists.
close_reason: Implemented in Phase B commit

title: Enhancement: Pre/post cycle hook scripts (user-defined extension points)
description:
## Finding
There is no mechanism for users to inject arbitrary PowerShell before or after the entire cycle (or before/after individual phases) without editing the orchestrator source. This is the most-requested extension point in peer tools (WAU `_WAU-mods.ps1`, Topgrade `[pre_commands]`/`[post_commands]`) because it covers every site-specific case: stop a service before updates, run a custom health script after, clear caches, notify a ticketing system, etc.

## Suggestion
Add `-PreCycleScript` and `-PostCycleScript` parameters accepting a file path or scriptblock. Optionally extend with a `hooks.psd1` sidecar exposing `BeforeWinget`, `AfterWindowsUpdate`, etc. (companion P2 issue covers the per-phase form).

## Peer reference
WAU mods system; Topgrade pre/post commands; Boxstarter chocolatey hooks.
close_reason: Implemented in Phase F commit

title: Bug: No concurrency guard — duplicate orchestrator instances corrupt shared state
description:
## Finding
There is no named mutex, lock file, or process-presence check before the orchestrator increments `$state.Iteration` and writes state. On a fast boot the SYSTEM scheduled task may start a second instance before the first has exited (e.g., a lingering process from the prior run that hit a long package-manager timeout). Both instances read the same Iteration value, both increment it, and both can call `shutdown.exe`. The atomic temp-rename pattern protects against torn writes but does nothing against a read-modify-write race between two concurrent processes.

## Where
`Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:1660-1664` (Iteration read-modify-write) and `Register-BootUpdateTaskForReboot` early-return at 1305-1307.

## Suggestion
Acquire a named `System.Threading.Mutex` (e.g., `Global\BootUpdateCycle`) at script start and release on exit. Abort with a log line if the mutex is already owned by another instance.
close_reason: Implemented in Phase B commit

title: Lab harness reported a converged cycle against a one-line guest log
description: Invoke-LabRow's monitor assigned the guest log with 'x = if (Test-Path log) { @(Get-Content log) }'. A one-line file makes that assign a String, not an array, because the statement output is enumerated on the way out. String -match returns a boolean and false.Count is 1, so Complete read 1, Passes read 1, Matched read true, and lines[-1] indexed a character. Found 2026-09-09 when row D on lab-b ended 80 seconds in with 'cycle complete after 1 pass(es)' against a log holding a single self-update line, and wrote summary.json with Completed true and Passes 0. Fixed the same day: every count goes through Where-Object, the array wrapper moved outside the if in both the monitor and the evidence block, and the completion break also requires Passes >= 1.
acceptance_criteria: A row whose guest log holds exactly one line reports Completed false and does not break out of the monitor loop. Filed closed: fixed in the same session, commit on master.
close_reason: Fixed in the same session it was found, commit 918f641. Invoke-LabRow assigned the guest log with 'x = if (Test-Path log) { @(Get-Content log) }', and a one-line file collapses that to a String on the way out of the if, so every downstream idiom lied at once: String -match returns a boolean and false.Count is 1, giving Complete=1, Passes=1, Matched=true and lines[-1] indexing a character. Row D ended 80 seconds in with 'cycle complete after 1 pass(es)' against a log holding one self-update line and wrote summary.json with Completed true and Passes 0. Every count now goes through Where-Object, which returns a collection whatever it is handed; the array wrapper moved outside the if in both the monitor and the evidence block; and the completion break additionally requires Passes >= 1, because a cycle cannot complete before it starts. Verified by reproducing the collapse directly (assigned type String, (\ -match 'COMPLETE').Count = 1, \[-1] = 'e') and confirming the fixed form yields Object[] and a count of 0.

title: ResumeUserSid preference is dead code; v2.5.78 notes claim it
description:
Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1 ~L6687 assigns $state.ResumeUserSid inside try { } catch { }, but neither the state constructor (~L1897) nor the add-if-missing normaliser (~L1959) declares the property. Assigning an undeclared property on a [pscustomobject] throws, and the empty catch swallows it, so $script:ResumeUserSid is always $null and -PreferredSid never fires. Row B passed only because Resolve-BootUpdateResumeAccount now returns the SID from the name path. AzureAD\ and MicrosoftAccount\ machines still degrade to SYSTEM-only. The v2.5.78 release note "it is now preferred" is therefore false and must be corrected in the v2.5.79 notes.

Fix: declare ResumeUserSid in the constructor and the normaliser. Add a test that drives the discovery through the STATE OBJECT (constructor -> discovery -> Resolve), not by calling the resolver directly - the direct-call tests are exactly why this was invisible. Found by the v2.5.78 two-axis review, confirmed by reproducing the throw.
close_reason: Fixed. ResumeUserSid is now declared in New-BootUpdateStateV2 and in the add-if-missing list in Update-BootUpdateStateSchema, so the assignment no longer throws into an empty catch and Resolve-BootUpdateResumeAccount finally receives a real -PreferredSid. The discovery was extracted from Invoke-BootUpdateCycle into Update-BootUpdateResumeIdentity with its console-user and LogonUI lookups as scriptblock parameters, because the reason this survived a release is that every existing test called the resolver directly with a SID it supplied itself. Evidence: five new tests in tests/RebootResilience.Tests.ps1 ('Resume identity discovery through the state object') walk constructor -> discovery -> resolver, including the headless case where only the '.\name' form and a SID are known; Invoke-Pester on that file is 231 passed / 0 failed. The original failure mode was reproduced directly: assigning an undeclared property on a [pscustomobject] throws 'The property ResumeUserSid cannot be found on this object', and the empty catch left it null. The false v2.5.78 note is recorded for correction in the v2.5.79 Corrections section. Commit af4c728.

title: KB5007651 reports Installed but stays applicable every pass
description: Lab row B: the WindowsUpdate phase logs 'Installed [1] Updates' for 'Update for Windows Security platform - KB5007651' on every pass, then the final convergence scan still reports it applicable. Either the Defender platform update genuinely applies out-of-band and WU re-offers it (environmental, and the updater should recognise the pattern rather than retry it), or the phase is counting an install that did not happen - which would be a verified-update truthfulness defect of the kind the project rules forbid. Decide which by checking whether the guest's Defender platform version under %ProgramData%\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Platform actually advances across a pass. This is what made row B unable to converge at all.
close_reason: Resolved: environmental re-offer, branch one of the decision rule, with the diagnosis and the lab cover to back it. DIAGNOSIS, evidence C:\HyperV\evidence\k610-diagnosis-20260909-083408 (before/after probes around one full row B on a cold baseline-no-autologon restore): AMProductVersion advanced 4.18.23110.3 -> 4.18.26080.3 and a Defender Platform directory 4.18.26080.3-0 appeared where the guest had none, so the install really changes the machine; Windows Update history gained five KB5007651 entries in that run, every one ResultCode 2; and the update was still applicable at the end. The row itself, C:\HyperV\evidence\B-k610-diagnosis-boot-upd-matrix-20260909-083604, is the FAIL this replaces: 6 passes, Completed false, state file and both tasks left, 45-minute timeout, four cycles of 'Installed [1] Updates' followed by 'Final WU scan: ...KB5007651' and 'convergence withheld'. FIX: an update that Windows Update itself records as installed successfully in this boot and still offers on the final scan is recorded as deferred inventory with kind ReofferedAfterSuccess, is not counted as a verified update and not counted as retry fuel, and the completion claim is qualified. Only ResultCode 2 qualifies, so a failed install stays retryable; convergence is now withheld on the count of UNEXPLAINED updates; a clean pass retracts the previous pass's observation. LAB COVER: C:\HyperV\evidence\B-k610-cgua-v2-boot-upd-matrix-20260909-095952 is a PASS - Completed true, 5 passes, RebootsClaimed 2 = RebootsObservedOS 2, StateFileRemains false, TasksRemaining 0, CbsPending false, ConsoleUser empty and ExplorerCount 0 throughout. The log carries 'Windows Update re-offer after success: KB5007651 installed successfully N time(s) since this boot (result code 2 ...). Recorded as deferred inventory rather than retried.', 'Windows Update convergence qualified', and the claim 'BOOT UPDATE CYCLE COMPLETE WITH DEFERRED INVENTORY | 28.6 min | 5 iteration(s) | 2 reboot(s) | 2 verified updates'. One defect in the fix was found by reading that log rather than the tests: the history date arrives from COM as UTC tagged Unspecified, so ToUniversalTime() added the local offset twice - visible as an 18:12:42Z timestamp for a 14:12:42Z install, and dangerous because the same shift could carry a pre-boot success across the since-this-boot line and suppress real work. Fixed in commit 5744a28. Commits 4385fd9 and 5744a28.

title: SYSTEM-context cycle dies at task registration when no user is logged on
description: With nobody interactively signed in, resume-user discovery falls back to LastLoggedOnSAMUser, which returns a '.\\name' form that cannot be translated to a SID. Register-ScheduledTask throws a terminating CimException, the cycle dies immediately after pre-flight, and NO continuation task is registered. Updates on a headless machine can therefore never proceed or resume.
design:
Found by VM matrix row B (-l6yq) on boot-upd-matrix, 2026-09-08, commit 7e7dcd0.

Evidence, captured by running the orchestrator directly as SYSTEM under a transcript:
  TerminatingError(Register-ScheduledTask): No mapping between account names and security IDs was done. (9,27):UserId:.\\updtest
  TERMINATING ERROR: No mapping between account names and security IDs was done.
  TYPE: Microsoft.Management.Infrastructure.CimException

Confirmed on the guest:
  LastLoggedOnSAMUser = '.\\updtest'
  ([NTAccount]'.\\updtest').Translate([SecurityIdentifier]) -> FAILS, 'Some or all identity references could not be translated'
  ([NTAccount]'UPDTESTVM\\updtest').Translate(...) -> S-1-5-21-...-1000, resolves fine
  Win32_ComputerSystem.UserName is empty, which is why the LogonUI fallback is reached at all.

Why it went unnoticed: the failure is invisible in the updater's own log. The last line written is 'Pre-flight: PROCEEDING'; the exception happens before the next Write-Log, and the orchestrator is launched as a child process by Deploy so its terminating error goes nowhere. Row B's first two attempts produced only 'exit code 1'. It took a transcript around a direct SYSTEM invocation to see it.

Severity: this is the whole SYSTEM-fallback path, which exists precisely for machines where nobody logs in. A state file is left behind and no continuation task is registered, so the cycle is not merely delayed - it is dead until someone intervenes.

Fix direction: normalise the discovered account before it reaches New-ScheduledTaskPrincipal / New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -User (expand a leading '.\\' to the computer name), and verify it translates to a SID. If it cannot be resolved, fall back to the SYSTEM-only registration branch that already exists rather than throwing - a machine with no resolvable user should still get its SYSTEM continuation.
acceptance_criteria: A cycle started as SYSTEM with no interactive user registers a continuation task and survives at least one reboot. An unresolvable resume user degrades to the SYSTEM-only branch instead of terminating. A regression test covers the '.\\name' form specifically, since that is what LogonUI actually returns.
close_reason: Fixed in d37d688 and verified by row B v3 on boot-upd-matrix. Task registration under SYSTEM with nobody signed in now succeeds: 'Scheduled task registered: BootUpdateCycle (UPDTESTVM\updtest at logon)'. The cycle then resumed across 4 real reboots as SYSTEM. Before the fix the same run died immediately after pre-flight with no continuation task at all. 375 unit tests pass including 5 covering the '.\name' form Windows actually returns.

title: Boot-session tolerance absorbs fast reboots, under-counting them and letting the reboot limit be evaded
description: Test-BootUpdateSameBootSession treats two boots within BootSessionToleranceSeconds (120) as the same boot session. The updater's own reboot cycle can complete in well under 120s, so a real reboot is absorbed: the completed-reboot counter does not increment, the completion claim under-reports, and because the counter gates the reboot limit, a fast reboot loop can run unbounded. That is this project's namesake failure.
design:
First evidence from VM matrix row A (-dei7) on boot-upd-matrix, 2026-09-08, running commit 58299ab.

Windows System event log, Event ID 6005, records THREE boots during the cycle: 15:40:41, 15:42:17, 15:43:36.
The updater logged 'Observed a new Windows boot session' only twice, at 15:41:25 (count 1) and 15:44:01 (count 2). Pass 3 at 15:42:44 recorded no new boot session and left Reboots at 1/5.
The missed pair 15:40:41 -> 15:42:17 is 96 seconds apart, inside the 120-second window.
Completion claim said '4 iteration(s) | 2 reboot(s)'. Three occurred.

The tolerance exists for a good reason: LastBootUpTime is derived and jitters by SECONDS within one boot, and exact comparison silently zeroes the same-boot retry budget (that is bug -d737376's territory). So the fix is not simply to shrink the window; jitter is seconds and fast reboots are tens of seconds, and those ranges overlap. The identity needs a signal that does not jitter.

Directions worth evaluating, none chosen yet:
- Count System event log 6005/6009 occurrences, which are per-boot facts rather than a derived timestamp.
- Compare system uptime (GetTickCount64): if uptime is less than the time elapsed since the pass that scheduled the shutdown, a reboot definitely happened.
- Have the updater write a per-boot GUID from its own startup task and compare that.
- Keep the tolerance for jitter but treat 'we scheduled a shutdown and the process restarted' as independent corroboration that a boot occurred.

Note the same tolerance also guards same-boot Windows Update evidence (Test-WindowsUpdateZeroEvidence) and the same-boot retry budget, so any change needs those regression tests re-run.
acceptance_criteria: Two reboots less than 120 seconds apart are both counted. The completed-reboot count in the completion claim equals the number of Event ID 6005 boots observed during the session. The reboot limit still fires after the configured number of genuinely fast reboots. Existing same-boot jitter protection still holds: repeated LastBootUpTime reads within one boot must not read as new sessions, and the same-boot retry budget must not reset.
close_reason:
2026-09-08 FIXED and verified on the VM lab, commit 7e7dcd0.

Verification run A-verify2-6qpf, boot-upd-matrix, checkpoint staged, 3 real pending reboots armed:
  RebootsClaimed 3, RebootsObservedOS 3 (Windows event 6005), RebootAccountingAgrees TRUE.
  4 passes, counts incrementing 1 -> 2 -> 3, completion claim "4 iteration(s) | 3 reboot(s)".
  Gaps between boots were 72s and 69s, both well inside the 120s LastBootUpTime tolerance that previously absorbed them.
  State file absent afterwards, both continuation tasks removed, CBS clear.

THE FIRST FIX WAS WRONG AND THE LAB CAUGHT IT. Attempt one compared raw uptime and asked whether it had run backwards. Verification returned claimed=2 observed=3: the miss simply moved from pass 3 to pass 4. Uptime only runs backwards when the earlier pass ran later in its boot than the current pass runs in its own, and on this guest every pass started about 40 seconds after its boot, so uptime went 40 -> 45 across a genuine restart. All four unit tests for that attempt passed, because they were written around the imagined case rather than the observed one.

The shipped fix reconstructs the boot instant by subtracting monotonic uptime from the current time. Within a boot that value is stable to well under a second because both terms advance together; across a boot it jumps by the downtime. It has no dependence on where in each boot the passes land. It also permits a tight 15-second tolerance, because the reconstructed instant does not jitter the way LastBootUpTime does, which cleanly separates jitter from a fast restart.

Regression cover includes a test built from the exact observed failure (uptime 40 -> 45 across a real reboot), so this specific mistake cannot return. Suite 370 passed, 0 failed.

title: Killing a package tree leaves out-of-tree installers running
description: Remove-ProcessTree kills only descendants of the launched provider process. msiexec.exe is parented to services.exe, so an MSI-backed package that gets timed out leaves its installer running. The next pass then collides with the Windows Installer mutex and every subsequent package fails 1618.
design: Observed 2026-09-06 in BootUpdateCycle.log. Winget-machine-Adobe.Acrobat.Reader.64-bit was killed at 13:03:07. At 13:22:09 the resumed pass logged 'Installers running: msiexec (PID 41352); TrustedInstaller; TiWorker', and msiexec 41352 was still present at 13:31:25. Six machine-scope packages (Amazon.AWSCLI, DoltHub.Dolt, TheDocumentFoundation.LibreOffice, JohnMacFarlane.Pandoc, Microsoft.WindowsPCHealthCheck and others) failed installer exit 0x00000652 = 1618 in that window. Cost: 3 iterations, 39.6 min. Note the kill itself was spurious - see the idle-detector fix - but the orphan hazard is independent and survives that fix. Options: detect a still-running msiexec/TrustedInstaller after a kill and wait for it rather than proceeding; or refuse to start the next package while the installer mutex is held.
acceptance_criteria: After a provider timeout kill, the cycle does not start another MSI-backed package while a system installer from the killed operation is still running, and 1618 is not produced by the updater's own orphan.
close_reason: Fixed. After either timeout kill in Wait-ProcessWithIdleTimeout, the cycle now calls Wait-BootUpdateInstallerMutex, which asks the question Windows Installer actually arbitrates - is Global\_MSIExecute held - and waits, bounded at 10 minutes, for the orphaned transaction to finish before the pass continues. Asking the mutex rather than looking for a running msiexec.exe is the point: msiexec runs as a service process for reasons unrelated to an active transaction, so a process-name wait would block on nothing, while the mutex is exactly what produces 1618. Killing the orphan was rejected deliberately: tearing down an MSI transaction mid-write is how a machine ends up with a half-installed product. The wait is bounded and reports both outcomes, so a pass that proceeds anyway can say the transaction was still held. Evidence: seven new tests in tests/RebootResilience.Tests.ps1, Describe 'A killed package tree does not race the installer it orphaned' - absent mutex and existing-but-free mutex both read as no transaction; a mutex held by another thread reads as in progress; the ordinary path pays nothing (zero UI waits, zero log lines); the wait returns the moment the holder releases; it gives up at the bound and warns; and the kill-then-wait ordering on both the HardTimeout and IdleTimeout paths is pinned against the function's own text, since waiting before the kill would wait on the transaction the cycle is about to terminate. The tests drive a private Local\\ mutex, never the machine-wide one, because creating Global\\_MSIExecute would make every real installer on the host believe an installation was in progress. Invoke-Pester tests/RebootResilience.Tests.ps1 = 257 passed / 0 failed. Not yet exercised on a lab guest; the matrix rows in Phase 3 and the final validation rows cover the kill paths. title: Deferred inventory must qualify the convergence claim
description:
The truthful-convergence invariant is violated today, independently of the Chocolatey quarantine work.

CONTEXT.md: deferred inventory "does not make a phase fail, but it does prevent an unqualified claim of convergence." The code implements only the first half.

Evidence, 2026-08-24 17:00 run (diagnostics bundle BootUpdateCycle-diagnostics-20260824-211933Z):
  17:00:35 [Warn] Winget machine: deferred inventory - 1 install-technology blocked.   (Microsoft.Edge)
  17:02:19 [Info] BOOT UPDATE CYCLE COMPLETE | 2.3 min | 1 iteration(s) | 0 reboot(s) | 1 verified updates
  17:02:26 [Info] Notification: toast sent (Success)

An unqualified convergence claim plus a Success toast, with deferred inventory outstanding.

Root cause: $deferredCount (Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:1119, Pinned + Unknown + TechnologyBlocked) is consumed solely by Test-WingetExitReconciled to decide the provider exit code was benign. It never propagates to Resolve-BootUpdateCompletionDisposition or to the completion claim. There is no disposition kind for "complete but not unqualifiedly converged."

Required per ADR-0003:
- Carry deferred inventory through to the completion claim.
- Qualify the log wording, the notification severity, and the repair plan.
- Do NOT change the exit code. Callers (upd.cmd, both scheduled tasks) read non-zero as failure, which would assert that a phase failed - the one thing the term forbids. Nothing failed; exit stays 0.
- Do not conflate deferred inventory with UserCompletionDeferred (a scope deferral, already wired to Kind='UserContext'). See the split in CONTEXT.md.

Note this is a visible behaviour change on machines silently carrying deferred inventory, including the dev machine via Edge (see -4ik).
notes:
IMPLEMENTED in 8ab5573. Deferred inventory now qualifies the completion claim per ADR-0003.

Seams added (all behaviour-tested, 33 new Pester cases):
- Get-BootUpdateCompletionClaim - qualifier set -> claim string; replaces the nested if/elseif that did not scale past two qualifiers. Normalises the inconsistent 'COMPLETE WITH QUARANTINE AND CLEANUP ADVISORY' to 'COMPLETE WITH WINGET QUARANTINE AND CLEANUP ADVISORY'. Safe: Export-BootUpdateDiagnostics matches 'BOOT UPDATE CYCLE COMPLETE\b' and nothing parses past the prefix, which the function guarantees stays first.
- Add-/Get-BootUpdateDeferredInventory - cycle-state backed, asserted across a ConvertTo-Json/ConvertFrom-Json round-trip as the safety rule requires, including the single-element-array-rehydrates-as-scalar trap.
- Get-BootUpdateDeferredInventorySummary and Get-BootUpdateCompletionNotification - toast severity is now a behaviour test, not a source grep.

Carriers wired: log line, toast severity (Success -> Progress), banner colour and lines, and Write-BootUpdateRepairPlan -DeferredInventory. Exit code unchanged at 0.

DEFECT CAUGHT IN REVIEW, fixed before commit: Write-WingetScopeSummary is also called with synthetic scope labels - "<scope>-retry" (lines 3077/3148) and "<scope>/<PackageId>" (line 3224). The first cut recorded those as ledger scopes, which double-reported a single deferral under a scope name that does not exist and stranded a "machine-retry" entry that nothing would ever clear, since an entry is only replaced by a summary carrying the identical label. Now records only 'user' and 'machine'; a retry that narrows a deferral is picked up by the next full-scope pass, erring toward reporting outstanding work rather than dropping it.

Two pre-existing source-text tests broke on the refactor with no behaviour change (RebootResilience 'reports durable Winget quarantine...', TuiExperience 'distinguishes completion, retry...'). Both re-pointed at the same invariants in their new homes rather than deleted.

GATES: unit-and-process-behavior PASS (357), user-system-security-boundary PASS, published-launcher-upgrade PASS. Live bootstrap, provider integration, and multi-reboot convergence NOT RUN - no disposable VM (see -3tw).

Verification still owed: this changes completion-claim behaviour, so the next real cycle on this machine should show 'COMPLETE WITH DEFERRED INVENTORY' and a non-Success toast whenever Edge is pending. That is the production confirmation; it has not been observed yet.

title: Persisted boot-session identity broke on JSON round-trip, making the same-boot retry budget unreachable
description:
State is persisted as JSON, and ConvertFrom-Json rehydrates ISO-8601 values as [datetime] (Kind=Utc). Test-BootUpdateSameBootSession declared its parameters as [string], so parameter binding rendered that [datetime] in the current culture and dropped the offset. Re-parsing then assumed the local offset, skewing the comparison by the machine's full UTC offset.

Reproduced against a live state file:
  ($raw | ConvertFrom-Json).LastBootSessionId.GetType()  -> System.DateTime (Kind=Utc)
  [string]$_                                             -> '08/24/2026 15:54:52'
  current                                                -> '2026-08-24T15:54:52.5000000Z'
  deltaSeconds                                           -> 14399.5   (tolerance: 120)

Every pass therefore reported a new boot session, and Update-BootUpdateStateForBootSession responded by zeroing ConsecutiveRetryCount, clearing ExplicitRebootRequests, and discarding WindowsUpdateZeroEvidence. MaxRetryPasses was unreachable, so a permanently failing phase retried indefinitely: session 2026-08-24 11:42:43 reached pass 7 and session 2026-08-22 22:48:52 reached pass 42, with no reboot in between in either case.

The jitter tolerance added for the 2026-07-27 diagnostics was itself correct; it was simply never reached.

Why existing tests missed it: the 'Jitter-tolerant boot session identity' block passed throughout. Every case fed Test-BootUpdateSameBootSession string literals, exercising the comparison but never the state-file boundary where the type actually changed.

Fix (commit d737376):
- ConvertTo-BootUpdateTimestampString normalises [datetime]/[datetimeoffset] back to round-trip 'o' form.
- Applied at the load boundary in Update-BootUpdateStateSchema for StartTime, LastRun, LastPhaseTimestamp, LastPreflightNetworkAt, LastBootSessionId, LimitReachedAt.
- Applied again inside Test-BootUpdateSameBootSession, whose parameters are no longer typed [string].
- Also covers WindowsUpdateZeroEvidence.ObservedAtUtc, read back via [datetime]::Parse([string]$_). Same defect class, milder symptom: evidence aged out an offset early, causing redundant Windows Update rescans.

Regression coverage: seven tests in tests/RebootResilience.Tests.ps1 under 'Boot session identity survives the state-file round-trip'. They round-trip state through ConvertTo-Json/ConvertFrom-Json before asserting, including a five-pass loop that reloads state each iteration and requires the budget to climb to 5 rather than reset.

Gates at time of fix: unit-and-process-behavior (314 passed), user-system-security-boundary, published-launcher-upgrade. All passed, none skipped.

Mirrored to GitHub as nanoDBA/boot-upd#50 while bd was unreachable (Smart App Control blocked bd.exe on 2026-08-24).
close_reason: Fixed in d737376: ConvertTo-BootUpdateTimestampString plus load-boundary normalisation, with seven round-trip regression tests. All three gates passed.

title: [P1] Empty PackageId crashes Winget phase in Complete-WingetFailureClassification
description:
## Problem

Diagnostics from 2026-08-24 (BootUpdateCycle-diagnostics-20260824-123130Z.zip) show the Winget phase
crashing with an uncaught PowerShell exception on v2.5.72 (current latest), e.g. 2026-08-19 08:15:46:

```
[Error] <<< [1/10] Winget - FAILED (4.3 min)
[Error]   Error: Cannot bind argument to parameter '"'"'PackageId'"'"' because it is an empty string.
[Error]   Stack:    at System.Management.Automation.ExceptionHandlingOps.CheckActionPreference(...)
   ... at Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.ForEachObjectCommand.ProcessScriptBlockParameterSet()
```

Note the "FAILED (4.3 min)" line has no ", N pkg" suffix -- that is the signature of the outer
phase try/catch at Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:6340-6350 catching an unhandled exception, not the
normal graceful phase-failure path (which always includes a pkg count).

## Root cause

`Get-WingetOutputSummary` (Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:1035) only sets `$currentId` when it sees a
"(N/M) Found Name [Id] Version V" header line first (line 1055). That numbered-counter header is
only emitted by winget during bulk `--all` enumeration. A targeted single-package upgrade
(`winget upgrade --id $pkgId ...`, used by the filtered/excluded-package code path at line 3012-3019)
does not print that header shape, so if such an invocation'"'"'s output produces an
"Installer failed with exit code: ..." line (1063), the resulting failure record is built with
`Id=`'"'"''"'"'` (line 1066-1072).

That empty-Id failure record later reaches `Complete-WingetFailureClassification`
(Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:1157-1162):

```powershell
Command=(Get-WingetRemediationCommand -PackageId $_.Id -Code $_.Code)
```

`Get-WingetRemediationCommand`'"'"'s `-PackageId` parameter is `[Parameter(Mandatory)][string]`.
PowerShell rejects an empty string for a Mandatory `[string]` parameter during binding, before the
function body (and its own internal `-notmatch` safety regex at line 1123) ever runs. The exception
is uncaught inside `Update-WingetPackages` and aborts the entire Winget phase.

This is a different code path from the fix in commit 866bb53 (closed issue
on_boot_update_reboot_loop_while_pending_restarts_exist-2a8l), which hardened the bulk `--all`
*inventory table* parser (`Get-WingetInventoryPackageIds`). That fix does not cover this
failure-record/remediation-command path, and the crash reproduces on v2.5.72 (the release that
included that fix).

## Acceptance criteria

- A Winget failure record with an empty/missing `Id` never reaches
  `Get-WingetRemediationCommand -PackageId` with an empty string; either guard the call site or
  make the parameter safely accept/reject empty values without throwing.
- The Winget phase completes gracefully (fails closed with a diagnostic, not an unhandled
  exception) when a failure record lacks a package ID.
- Pester coverage: a fixture where `Get-WingetOutputSummary` sees an "Installer failed with exit
  code" line with no preceding "(N/M) Found ... [Id]" header, feeding into
  `Complete-WingetFailureClassification`, must not throw and must produce a sane remediation
  Details entry (e.g. `Command = $null`).
- `./tools/Invoke-TestGates.ps1` passes.
close_reason: Fixed in commit (pending); Get-WingetRemediationCommand no longer takes a Mandatory empty-rejecting PackageId, guarded with AllowEmptyString/AllowNull. Pester 307/307, cross-context-mutex, and published-launcher-upgrade gates pass.

title: [P1] Make targeted Winget inventory parsing reject prose and empty package IDs
description:
## Problem

The 2026-08-09 diagnostic shows targeted Winget inventory parsing treating provider prose as a package identifier:

```
Winget (machine/n numbers that cannot be determ) returned ... 0x8A150014
Error: Cannot bind argument to parameter 'PackageId' because it is an empty string.
```

The current fixed-column parser accepts any non-dash text extracted from rows after the table header. Winget footer/status lines can therefore become package IDs, and malformed/short rows can reach a mandatory `PackageId` parameter.

## Reliability impact

- Executes pointless per-package calls against fabricated IDs.
- Can abort the entire Winget phase with a PowerShell binding error.
- Obscures the real provider result and damages retry classification.

## Acceptance criteria

- Only syntactically valid Winget IDs are admitted from the table (same allowlist boundary used for remediation commands, or a stricter documented parser).
- Footer/status/progress/prose lines are never treated as package rows.
- Empty, truncated, or malformed rows are skipped without invoking a package mutation.
- If the table cannot be parsed confidently, the phase fails closed with one explicit diagnostic; it does not silently fabricate IDs.
- Fixture-based tests cover the observed “version numbers that cannot be determined” footer, short rows, localized/unrecognized output, and an empty ID.
- Logs retain the raw provider transcript for diagnosis without echoing unsafe text into commands.
close_reason: Implemented in commit 866bb53; focused Pester 145/145 and all non-integration suites 299/299 pass without running the live cycle or rebooting.

title: [bug] Same-boot retry budget silently reset by LastBootUpTime jitter, producing an unbounded recovery loop

title: Enhancement: Self-update of orchestrator from GitHub release tag
description:
## Finding
After deployment, the script in `$env:ProgramData\BootUpdateCycle` is frozen at the version pasted. Bug fixes and new phase support never reach a deployed instance without manual re-paste. This defeats "install once, forget".

## Suggestion
At cycle start, compare embedded `$ScriptVersion` against latest GitHub release tag via `Invoke-RestMethod https://api.github.com/repos/nanoDBA/boot-upd/releases/latest`. If newer, download the asset, validate SHA, overwrite, re-exec. Gate behind `-DisableSelfUpdate`.

## Peer reference
WAU auto-fetches its own latest release from GitHub by default (controllable via `DISABLEWAUAUTOUPDATE`).
close_reason: Implemented in Phase G commit

title: Enhancement: Defender signature update phase
description:
## Finding
Running Windows Update can temporarily disable/restart Defender. The cycle has no explicit `Update-MpSignature` step at the end, so a machine just out of a long power-off may exit the loop with stale AV definitions.

## Suggestion
Add late phase (after Windows Update, before final reboot check): `Update-MpSignature -UpdateSource MicrosoftUpdateServer`. Log the resulting `(Get-MpComputerStatus).AntivirusSignatureLastUpdated`. Returns Success regardless of outcome (signatures themselves don't trigger reboot).
close_reason: Implemented in Phase D commit

title: Enhancement: WSL kernel and distro package updates
description:
## Finding
Developer machines running WSL2 finish the cycle with a freshly-patched Windows kernel while the Ubuntu/Debian distro inside accumulates months of `apt` backlog — a real security gap.

## Suggestion
Opt-in `-UpdateWsl` switch (user-scoped, skipped under SYSTEM). Run `wsl --update --no-distribution` for the kernel; enumerate distros via `wsl --list --quiet` and invoke distro-appropriate package manager (`apt-get`, `dnf`, `pacman`). Capture exit code + count.

## Peer reference
Topgrade Windows runs include WSL kernel + per-distro updates.
close_reason: Implemented in Phase D commit

title: Enhancement: Metered connection detection (skip or warn on cellular/hotspot)
description:
## Finding
Pre-flight checks reachability but not metered status. On a laptop reconnecting via mobile hotspot, the orchestrator happily downloads hundreds of MB.

## Suggestion
Add to pre-flight: `Get-NetConnectionProfile` IsMetered check, or use the WinRT `NetworkInformation` API. Abort or warn (configurable). Add `-AllowMetered` opt-out flag.

## Peer reference
WAU detects metered connections and aborts by default with override.

title: Enhancement: Driver and firmware update opt-in (PSWindowsUpdate -Category Drivers/Firmware)
description:
## Finding
The Windows Update phase excludes SQL Server but does not run a separate pass for `-Category "Drivers"` / `"Firmware"` updates that sit in the Optional Updates queue. On fresh-built or hardware-changed machines, chipset/NIC/GPU/firmware updates are silently skipped.

## Suggestion
Add an opt-in `-IncludeDriverUpdates` switch (default `$false`); when set, run a second `Get-WindowsUpdate -Category 'Drivers'` (and optionally `'Firmware'`) call before the reboot-check. Default off to avoid instability on production servers.

## Peer reference
PSWindowsUpdate categories; Patch My PC enterprise catalog.

title: Enhancement: Parallelize Winget user-scope and machine-scope passes
description:
## Finding
Winget runs user-scope then machine-scope sequentially (lines 651-681). Each scope can take 5-15 min on activity-heavy machines. The two scopes operate on disjoint package metadata roots and can safely run concurrently.

## Where
`Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:651-681`

## Suggestion
Launch both scopes as background jobs simultaneously via `Invoke-PackageManagerWithTimeout` parallelized at the scope level; aggregate their `@{ Success; Count }` results.

## Estimated savings
~15-25% of total cycle wall-clock on the first iteration (the only run that does both scopes).
close_reason: Implemented in Phase C commit

title: Bug: State file .tmp leak when Move-Item fails post-write
description:
## Finding
`Set-BootUpdateState` writes to a `.tmp` file then `Move-Item -Force`. If the rename fails (file lock, ACL flip, transient I/O error) AFTER the temp is written, the `.tmp` file persists in `$env:ProgramData\BootUpdateCycle`. Subsequent runs ignore the stray file but it accumulates noise and can mask the real state file in a manual inspection. No cleanup of stale `.tmp` files on subsequent successful writes.

## Where
`Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:259-268` (Set-BootUpdateState)

## Suggestion
On entry to `Set-BootUpdateState`, check for and remove any pre-existing `<state>.tmp` from a prior failed write. Also surface Move-Item failures as a logged error rather than swallowing.
close_reason: Fixed in commit ae8b616 (Phase A bug-fix batch)

title: Bug: Register-BootUpdateTaskForReboot early-returns when task exists — stale args silently inherited
description:
## Finding
The function returns early if a task with name `BootUpdateCycle` already exists, without comparing arguments. If the user re-runs Deploy with new `-ExcludePatterns`, `-MaxIterations`, `-WebhookUrl`, etc., the next post-reboot iteration silently inherits the prior task's arguments. The `Register-ScheduledTask -Force` overwrite further down is correct but unreachable.

## Where
`Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:1303-1347` (specifically the early-return at 1305-1307)

## Suggestion
Either (a) remove the early-return so `-Force` always rewrites the action; or (b) compare the existing task's action arguments with the desired arguments and re-register if they differ.
close_reason: Fixed in commit ae8b616 (Phase A bug-fix batch)

title: Bug: Iteration counter incremented BEFORE maintenance-window gate — burns iterations on misses
description:
## Finding
`$state.Iteration++` and `Set-BootUpdateState` execute at lines 1661-1664, **before** the maintenance-window check at line 1696 which can `exit 0`. On a machine with a narrow maintenance window, every out-of-window boot consumes one iteration slot. With default `MaxIterations=5` and a 1-hour window, 5 out-of-window boots can exhaust the counter without ever running an update phase, then the cycle aborts with "Max iterations exceeded" and self-destructs.

## Where
`Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:1661-1664` vs `:1696-1699`

## Suggestion
Move the `$state.Iteration++` / `Set-BootUpdateState` block to AFTER the maintenance-window gate passes. Splash/banner can use a probe iteration value, then commit only on actual run.
close_reason: Fixed in commit ae8b616 (Phase A bug-fix batch)

title: Bug: pip per-package upgrade — name passed unquoted and ExcludePatterns not applied
description:
## Finding
`& pip install --upgrade $pkg.name` passes the name unquoted and skips ExcludePatterns filtering entirely. Names with brackets (`boto3[crt]`) or any whitespace from a malformed `pip list --outdated --format=json` row split into multiple args, causing pip to interpret the second word as a separate package to upgrade. The exclude-pattern feature documented for users does not apply here, surprising users who configured it to skip e.g. a pinned `numpy`.

## Where
`Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:888-892`

## Suggestion
Quote the name: `& pip install --upgrade "$($pkg.name)"`. Apply ExcludePatterns filtering analogous to the winget/choco paths.

title: Bug: ExcludePatterns regex-injected into Windows Update NotTitle filter
description:
## Finding
`Install-WindowsUpdates` builds the NotTitle filter as `((@("SQL") + $script:ExcludePatterns) -join "|")`, concatenating user-supplied strings directly into a regex alternation passed to PSWindowsUpdate. A pattern like `Microsoft.NET` is interpreted as "Microsoft, then any char, then NET" and silently over-excludes; a pattern containing `(`, `+`, or `[` may throw deep inside the module.

## Where
`Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:858`

## Suggestion
Escape each user pattern with `[regex]::Escape()` before joining: `(@("SQL") + ($script:ExcludePatterns | ForEach-Object { [regex]::Escape($_) })) -join "|"`.

## Related
Companion to closed #13 (substring matching) and #16 (special-char escaping in task args). This one is the regex-side analog.
close_reason: Fixed in commit ae8b616 (Phase A bug-fix batch)

title: Bug: Save-CycleHistory write is non-atomic and has no parse error handling
description:
## Finding
State writes use the safe temp+rename pattern, but the history write at `Save-CycleHistory` uses plain `Set-Content`. If power is lost mid-write — the exact scenario this orchestrator runs to recover from — the history JSON is truncated and all entries are lost. The subsequent `ConvertFrom-Json` on the partial file throws and is never caught; cleanup aborts. Independently, a fresh-install / empty file path also throws on `ConvertFrom-Json $null`.

## Where
`Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:316-319` (Save-CycleHistory).

## Suggestion
1. Wrap `ConvertFrom-Json` in try/catch; on failure start with empty array and log a warning.
2. Mirror the `Set-BootUpdateState` pattern: write to `<path>.tmp` then `Move-Item -Force`.
close_reason: Fixed in commit ae8b616 (Phase A bug-fix batch)

title: Bug: shutdown.exe /c comment passed unquoted — risk of arg splitting on legacy native passing
description:
## Finding
`& shutdown.exe /r /f /t $script:RebootDelaySec /c $shutdownComment /d p:2:17` passes a multi-word comment unquoted. Under PS7.3+ default `$PSNativeCommandArgumentPassing = "Standard"` PowerShell auto-quotes args with spaces, but on PS7.0-7.2 the default is Legacy and the comment splits on the first space — `shutdown.exe`'s logged comment becomes just `Boot`. Future modifications that add `"` or `\` to the comment also break.

## Where
`Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:1920`

## Suggestion
Wrap the comment with explicit quotes: `/c "$shutdownComment"` — or set `$PSNativeCommandArgumentPassing = 'Standard'` explicitly at the top of the script.
close_reason: Fixed in commit ae8b616 (Phase A bug-fix batch)

title: Bug: $SkipDotnetTools defaults ON (switch declared bare); contradicts docs/CLAUDE.md
description:
## Finding
`Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:54` declares `[switch]$SkipDotnetTools` with no default. PowerShell `[switch]` defaults to `$false` when absent — meaning the .NET global tools update phase **runs by default**. The CLAUDE.md architecture table, the in-file `*** HIGH RISK ***` warning, and the README all say "OFF by default", which is the opposite of current behavior. .NET global tool upgrades have a high failure rate (SDK pinning, breaking minor bumps) and were intentionally meant to be opt-in.

## Where
`Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:54`

## Suggestion
Change to `[switch]$SkipDotnetTools = $true`.
close_reason: Fixed in commit ae8b616 (Phase A bug-fix batch)

title: Harden unattended lab setup operations with bounded readiness and retry
description:
Unattended lab setup resilience follow-up

Harness/setup observations, not updater lifecycle failures:

- An optional-feature CBS arm failed when the PowerShell Direct channel disconnected before the updater launched.
- A guest module-copy setup step failed with a device-not-ready result before deployment.
- A prepared harness now uses three bounded 10-second guest-copy retries, and a fresh rerun completed through the retry path.

Follow-up:

- Add bounded readiness and retry handling for idempotent setup operations such as guest file transfer.
- Do not blindly retry non-idempotent feature arming; classify the operation and preserve a safe retry boundary.
- Emit durable, stage-specific setup diagnostics with elapsed time and sanitized failure details.
- Preserve failed guest evidence and the setup stage that failed so later analysis can distinguish harness/setup failure from updater lifecycle failure.

The separate online prerequisite acquisition concern is tracked independently in GitHub #65 and is outside this issue's scope.

Acceptance criteria:

- A deterministic setup fixture exercises readiness loss and recovers with bounded retry for an idempotent operation.
- A non-idempotent feature-arm failure is recorded with an explicit no-blind-retry outcome.
- Failed setup retains the relevant guest evidence and a durable stage record without private host, user, or path identifiers.
- A successful prepared rerun and a bounded-failure case are covered by harness tests.

title: Resolve lab credential analyzer errors blocking quality CI
description:
The quality workflow for commit 7230e48 fails its recursive PSScriptAnalyzer error gate on five pre-existing lab credential findings: plaintext-to-SecureString conversions in Invoke-LabRow, LabCredential, New-LabGuest and New-LabHeadlessCheckpoint, plus the username/password parameter pair in Set-BootUpdLabPassword. Preserve existing Windows Credential Manager behavior and never print/store raw secrets in tracked artifacts. Validate with the exact CI analyzer command, focused credential tests and the existing relevant compatibility gates.

title: Bound required-module acquisition before updater initialization
description:
In the September 12 headless VM run, the SYSTEM deployment task started and remained running before any updater cycle/state/log existed. Captured output stayed at Installing module: PSWindowsUpdate... for an extended setup interval. The guest had only PowerShellGet and PackageManagement 1.0.0.1, no discovered NuGet provider, and no PSWindowsUpdate module. A separate guest-user reachability probe got a WebException from the PowerShell Gallery package endpoint while the NuGet index returned HTTP 200; this does not by itself establish the SYSTEM request's exact failure.

Deploy-BootUpdateCycle.ps1 calls Install-Module for required modules before updater initialization, without an explicit setup timeout or a durable failure/status artifact. The in-flight watchdog is not yet armed. The test therefore cannot exercise lifecycle behavior until dependency acquisition finishes, and normal updater diagnostics do not describe this interval.

Add bounded, noninteractive required-module acquisition with recorded stage, elapsed time and sanitized actionable failure details. Preserve normal installs and reuse existing verified modules. Do not silently skip required capabilities or claim updater completion. Test a deterministic stalled/failing gallery/provider-bootstrap seam and a successful acquisition path, plus SYSTEM deployment from a prepared VM.

Source validation task: #62. This is a VM-discovered deployment/setup issue, separate from the corrected cleanup-manifest defect #53.
acceptance_criteria: Required-module acquisition has a bounded noninteractive timeout and durable sanitized stage/failure evidence; deterministic stalled/failing and successful acquisition cases tested; SYSTEM setup cannot wait silently without an actionable outcome.
notes: Subsequent observation at 15:08:58Z showed deployment advancing to BurntToast installation. This is not a proven permanent PSWindowsUpdate hang or a demonstrated SYSTEM networking failure; the open scope is bounded setup and durable diagnostics.

title: Add terminal evidence for interrupted or unclosed update cycles
description:
GitHub follow-up: #47

An update-cycle diagnostic bundle contains a user-context phase that stops reporting after a heartbeat, with no idle timeout, hard timeout, child-exit record, completion marker, or explicit abort marker before a later run starts. The later run completed successfully, so this does not prove that the package phase is permanently broken. It does show that an interrupted or orphaned cycle can leave an unclosed interval without enough evidence to distinguish watchdog termination, parent termination, host shutdown, or logging failure. This description preserves the historical report; it is not a claim that the event has been newly reproduced.

This overlaps partially with closed Beads issue on_boot_update_reboot_loop_while_pending_restarts_exist-35qb.10, which addressed a killed mid-pass cycle not resuming until a later logon or boot. The present scope is broader: terminal evidence and process-tree outcome classification for interrupted or unclosed cycles, including the next-invocation annotation.

Acceptance criteria:

- Record an explicit terminal outcome for parent cancellation, process-tree kill, child-start failure, and unexpected parent termination.
- Ensure the watchdog or heartbeat path cannot silently stop reporting while a child remains active; record the last observed process-tree state when it exits.
- On the next invocation, detect and annotate an unfinished prior cycle without treating it as successful completion or creating duplicate resume work.
- Add a deterministic regression fixture for an unclosed child phase and verify exported diagnostics preserve the distinction.

title: Diagnostics: empty cleanup endpoints incorrectly report Persistent=true
description:
The 20260912-142250 diagnostics manifest reports PendingFileCleanup.Persistent=true while BeforeMutation and AfterUpdates both have Observation=observed-empty, Categories={}, Fingerprints=[], Pass=2. This falsely labels a fully empty queue as persistent cleanup.

Positive control with identical nonempty fingerprints yields true; cleared nonempty-to-empty yields false. title: A cycle killed mid-pass is not resumed until the next logon or boot
description: Found by matrix row G on 2026-09-09, evidence C:\HyperV\evidence\G-killed-after-promotion-v2-boot-upd-matrix-20260909-110032 and C:\Lab\g4-kill-evidence.json on the guest. The orchestrator was killed during the WindowsUpdate phase of pass 1, after Winget and Chocolatey had been promoted into the state file. State integrity held perfectly: the state file parsed before and after, no .tmp remained, and PhaseAfter=WindowsUpdate with WingetDone and ChocolateyDone both true, so a resuming pass would correctly skip the completed work. Nothing resumed. Both continuation tasks sat Ready for the remainder of the 40-minute row and no further pass ran. The resume chain armed at the start of a pass is entirely boot- and logon-scoped: BootUpdateCycle triggers at logon and BootUpdateCycleFallback at startup+3min, so on a machine that is already logged on and does not reboot, a crashed or killed cycle stalls indefinitely. Task Scheduler's RestartOnFailure (3 x 2 minutes) does not cover it either when the pass was launched by Deploy-BootUpdateCycle.ps1 or upd.cmd rather than by the BootUpdateCycle task, which is always the case for the FIRST pass - and that is the pass this row killed. Note this is not the same defect as the missing dated watchdog fixed in f74b693: that one covered the shutdown /a escape hatch on the restart path only. Likely shape of the fix: arm a repeating watchdog trigger (for example -Once with a RepetitionInterval) when the resume checkpoint is armed, so a probe runs periodically while a cycle is in flight, exits immediately on the existing named mutex when the cycle is healthy, and resumes it when it is not. Deliberately NOT done in v2.5.79: it introduces a repeating scheduled task into the resume chain and would need its own lab row to validate, and shipping it on the strength of a green unit suite is the exact failure mode this release exists to correct.
acceptance_criteria: After the orchestrator is killed mid-pass on a machine that stays logged on and does not reboot, a later pass starts on its own within a bounded and documented interval, resumes at the correct phase, and does not re-run phases already marked done. Demonstrated by a lab row, not by the unit suite.
notes: Deferred out of v2.5.79 deliberately. The fix puts a repeating watchdog trigger into the resume chain, which changes what every continuation task looks like, and it would need its own lab row to validate. Shipping it on the strength of a green unit suite is the exact failure mode this release exists to correct. The gap is pre-existing, not a regression, and is stated plainly in the v2.5.79 notes.

title: NoInteractiveUser exhaustion branch has no test
description:
The bounded-wait exhaustion branch (~L7670-7685: Add-BootUpdateDeferredInventory Kind=NoInteractiveUser, then Phase=Running and fall-through to the completion path) has no test; only Update-BootUpdateUserIdentityWait, the counter, is covered. grep NoInteractiveUser tests/ returns nothing. Pair with -cgua for lab cover once row B can converge.

Four new tests in tests/RebootResilience.Tests.ps1, Describe 'No interactive user exhausts the bounded wait and completes with deferred inventory': (a) the bound fires only after MaxUserIdentityWaits rediscovery attempts and the resulting record is NoInteractiveUser in user scope for every deferred provider, surviving the state-file round trip; (b) the completion claim is 'COMPLETE WITH DEFERRED INVENTORY' and the toast is Progress, names 'Winget user (NoInteractiveUser=1)' and does not say 'you are all set'; (c) the exhausted branch sets Phase back to Running and does NOT call Register-BootUpdateTaskForReboot, so it hands the run to the same completion path whose cleanup-then-verify-then-notify ordering is already pinned in 'Evidence-backed completion'. title: Beads export writes a real name and email into a public repository
description:
.beads/issues.jsonl carries "assignee" and "owner" fields holding the maintainer's real name and email, and every export adds more rows (198 pre-existing, 5 added in v2.5.78). .claude/rules/public-repository-privacy.md: never publish real usernames; CLAUDE.md: treat all tracked content as public. title: Deepen boot-session identity into one module with one interface
description:
The boot-session identity cluster has now produced the same defect class twice (v2.5.74-era offset loss on LastBootSessionId, and the v2.5.78 fix for LastMonotonicBootId). Both times the cause was the shape of the interface, not the logic: callers gather three readings via three getters, hand raw timestamps to Update-BootUpdateStateForBootSession, and then re-derive the new-boot decision at the logging site. The invariant 'normalise a persisted timestamp before comparing it' lives in the caller's head, and the interface lets a new signal bypass the normaliser - which is exactly what happened.

Target shape: one call, one result, readings taken inside.

  $observation = Update-BootUpdateBootSession -State $state    # or -Reading $r in tests
  # { NewBoot; Reason: identity|monotonic|null; RebootCounted; State }

- External seam: callers pass state and consume the observation. They no longer know timestamps exist, so they cannot mishandle one. The logging site uses the result instead of mirroring the decision.
- Internal seam: Get-BootUpdateBootReading returns { SessionId; UptimeSeconds; MonotonicBootId }. Tests construct readings directly; production takes the real one. Two adapters vary across it, so it is a real seam, private to the module.
- Normalisation, both tolerances (120s identity, 15s monotonic), the anchoring policy (LastBootSessionId anchored, LastMonotonicBootId rewritten each pass), the Phase-gated reboot increment and the ConsecutiveRetryCount reset all live in one place.

Explicitly out of scope: dropping the CIM LastBootUpTime signal. Row B was decided entirely by the monotonic instant, so it may no longer earn its place, but that is a separate decision needing its own evidence and must not ride along with a restructure.

ACCEPTANCE - lab evidence is required, not optional. The unit suite has twice agreed with a change to this cluster while the lab disagreed, so a green Pester run is not sufficient to close this:
1. All existing round-trip tests pass, and the new-shape tests round-trip through real JSON with every persisted field populated.
2. Lab row A (interactive user, ArmReboots 3) passes with RebootsClaimed equal to RebootsObservedOS, and each reboot observed exactly once, including reboots inside the 120s tolerance. v2.5.78 baseline: 3 reboots 67s and 58s apart, each observed once.
3. Lab row B (headless, -MaxRetryPasses 3) stops itself at the recovery limit after 4 passes with the new-boot observation firing exactly once per real reboot. v2.5.78 baseline: evidence dir B-headless-terminal-v5.
4. Evidence directories for both rows are named in the closing comment.

Update-BootUpdateBootSession takes state and returns { NewBoot, Reason, RebootCounted, State }; normalisation, the 120-second identity tolerance and the 15-second monotonic one, the anchoring policy, the phase-gated reboot increment and the ConsecutiveRetryCount reset all live inside it. Get-BootUpdateBootReading is the internal seam a test varies and production does not. The cycle makes one call and logs what that call decided, so the logging site no longer re-derives the decision from raw timestamps it gathered itself. Update-BootUpdateStateForBootSession is retained as a shim with no logic of its own, so the existing round-trip tests keep checking the rules independently of the restructure. ACCEPTANCE: (1) all existing round-trip tests pass and the new-shape tests round-trip through real JSON with LastBootSessionId rehydrating as [datetime] - 478 tests, 0 failed. (2) Row A, C:\HyperV\evidence\A-v2579-final-boot-upd-matrix-20260909-145814: PASS, four passes, RebootsClaimed 3 = RebootsObservedOS 3, each boot observed exactly once, no state file, no tasks. Two of the three reboots were 103 and 74 seconds apart - inside the 120-second tolerance - and were detected by the monotonic signal, which the log now names: 'Observed a new Windows boot session (monotonic); completed reboot count is now 3.' title: Windows Update phase never completes when wuauserv is stopped under SYSTEM
description: On a guest where wuauserv is Stopped, every pass logs 'WU service: Stopped; bounded recovery is deferred to the Windows Update phase', the WindowsUpdate phase never completes, and verification is withheld indefinitely. Observed across 8 passes and 4 reboots without convergence.
design:
Seen in VM matrix row B v3, boot-upd-matrix, 2026-09-08, running as SYSTEM with nobody signed in.

The updater's behaviour is truthful throughout - it withholds the completion claim rather than asserting convergence it cannot support, which is what ADR-0003 asks for. The question is whether the bounded recovery the message promises actually runs and restarts the service, or whether the deferral simply loops.

Every pass repeats the same warning, and the cycle retried for 40 minutes over 4 real reboots without the phase completing, so on this evidence the recovery is either not firing or not succeeding under SYSTEM. Worth distinguishing: is wuauserv genuinely unstartable on this LTSC image, or is the recovery path not attempting it in SYSTEM context?

Note this is exactly the shape of the pre-existing -gtr work on provider convergence, and may be the same root.
acceptance_criteria: Either the WindowsUpdate phase's bounded recovery demonstrably starts wuauserv and completes the phase, or the cycle stops for manual attention with a message naming the stopped service, instead of retrying indefinitely.
close_reason: INVALID as written. A stopped wuauserv is the resting state on this LTSC image, not a defect state: Test-WindowsUpdateServiceReady starts the service on each pass, and pre-flight in later rows logs 'WU service: Running'. The row B v3 symptom this ticket generalised from was not the service failing to start; it was the WindowsUpdate phase never completing because KB5007651 reports Installed and stays applicable on every scan. That is -k610, which owns the real cause and the fix.

title: VM matrix G: killed-process recovery during checkpoint write and after state promotion
description: Kill the orchestrator at the two documented danger points: mid checkpoint creation, and immediately after state promotion. Confirm the next pass recovers rather than corrupting or re-running completed work.
design:
Reset with: Restore-VMCheckpoint -VMName boot-upd-matrix -Name updater-staged -Confirm:$false

Capture the guest console with C:\HyperV\Get-VmScreen.ps1 at each decision point and attach it as evidence. The on-screen clock doubles as a liveness check: compare it to the capture time.
acceptance_criteria: After each kill: the state file is either the old valid version or the new valid version, never a torn one; the next pass resumes at the correct phase; completed provider phases are not re-run; the resume chain still fires.
close_reason: PARTIAL, with the two halves reported separately because they came out differently. Evidence C:\HyperV\evidence\G-killed-after-promotion-v2-boot-upd-matrix-20260909-110032 plus C:\Lab\g4-kill-evidence.json on the guest. The orchestrator was killed during the WindowsUpdate phase of pass 1, after Winget and Chocolatey had been promoted into the state file, with no reboot armed. ESTABLISHED: the state file is never torn. It parsed valid immediately before and immediately after the kill, no .tmp file remained, and the post-kill state read Phase=WindowsUpdate, Iteration=1, WingetDone=true, ChocolateyDone=true - so the promotion of the completed phases survived and a resuming pass would correctly skip them. The kill also matched the right process for the first time: PID 7812, the Deploy-launched pwsh. The v2.5.77 attempt matched nothing because it looked for 'Invoke-BootUpdateCycle' in the command line, and only RESUMED passes are launched that way; the first pass runs Deploy-BootUpdateCycle.ps1. NOT ESTABLISHED: that the resume chain fires. Nothing ran for the remaining 37 minutes; summary.json is Completed false, Passes 1, TasksRemaining 2, StateFileRemains true. The chain armed at pass start is entirely boot- and logon-scoped - BootUpdateCycle at logon, BootUpdateCycleFallback at startup+3min - so on a machine already logged on that does not reboot, a killed cycle stalls indefinitely; and Task Scheduler's RestartOnFailure does not cover a pass launched by Deploy or upd rather than by the task, which is always true of the first pass. The two acceptance clauses that depend on a resume (resumes at the correct phase, completed phases not re-run) are therefore NOT RUN rather than passed, though the state contents show what a resume would have found. Filed as -35qb.10 with the likely fix (a repeating watchdog trigger armed with the resume checkpoint), deliberately not taken in v2.5.79: it puts a repeating scheduled task into the resume chain and needs its own lab row, and shipping it on a green unit suite is the failure mode this release exists to correct. Two earlier attempts, recorded so they are not repeated: v2 killed at the resume-checkpoint moment with -ArmReboots 1 and raced a restart already in flight, so 'killed' could not be distinguished from 'rebooted'; v3's injection scriptblock used try/catch as an expression, which PowerShell does not allow, so nothing was killed - the harness then reported Injected=true anyway, which is fixed in commit 0651d8c.

FIRST RUN AGAINST THE OLD BUILD, C:\HyperV\evidence\C-cancelled-restart-v3-lab-b-20260909-101428: FAIL.
