title: Three TuiExperience progress tests fail or flake on clean master
description: tests/TuiExperience.Tests.ps1 has two consistently failing tests and one flaky test on unmodified master. They were failing before the idle-detector work and are unrelated to it.
design: Confirmed by stashing all production changes and running against HEAD 704027f. (1) 'captures partial output and kills a silent native process tree at timeout' (line ~587): fails consistently, \ is null - the child's CHILD_PID line is never captured. TimeoutMinutes is 0.02 (1.2s), which is close to pwsh cold-start time, so the child may not print before the kill. Worth deciding whether this is a too-tight test deadline or a genuine loss of partial output on timeout, since capturing partial output is the behaviour the test is named for. (2) 'keeps animating while a silent external process produces no output' (line ~548): fails consistently, expects exactly 4 unique status strings, observed 8. (3) 'keeps animating through the production background-operation adapter' (line ~532): same exact-count assertion, flaky - 4 of 5 runs passed, one produced 8. The unique-status count depends on how many polls land in each 0.1-minute rounding bucket, so an exact equality is over-specified; more unique statuses means more animation, which is what the test name asks for. Note these assertions also become sensitive to the idle detector now reporting real CPU in the status string, so fix the assertions before that interaction is mistaken for a regression.
acceptance_criteria: The three tests pass repeatedly on master, asserting animation liveness rather than an exact unique-status count, and the partial-output expectation is either met or restated with a defensible deadline.
close_reason: Fixed in bd8f81e. Two tests asserted an exact count of four distinct rendered status lines, but the line embeds live CPU, process count, idle and elapsed readings, so the count depends on 0.1-unit rounding boundaries; they now assert the propeller cycles all four frames, which is deterministic and is the animation claim the tests name. The adapter test's operation grew 450ms to 1500ms so it outlasts a 1s poll interval. The third test's deadline was 1.2s while the nested pwsh needs a measured 4.0s to start and flush its first line, so the partial-output assertion could never pass; deadline is now 12s, still far below the child's 30s sleep. No production defect: output is read from the temp file after the wait returns, including on the timeout path. Full gates now green - 363 Pester passed 0 failed, cross-context-mutex passed, published-launcher-upgrade passed.

title: [bug] Explicit 3010/1641 short-circuit skips pending-file cleanup recording entirely
description:
Get-ConfirmedPendingReboot (Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:2504) short-circuits on an explicit reboot request before it ever probes pending-file state:

    if ($script:ExplicitRebootRequests.Count -gt 0) {
        return @($script:ExplicitRebootRequests)      # :2510
    }
    $first = @(Test-PendingReboot)
    Write-PendingFileRenameAdvisory -Operations $script:LastPendingFileRenameOperations -Context $Context   # :2515

Consequence: whenever any installer returns 3010 or 1641, Test-PendingReboot never runs for that context, $script:LastPendingFileRenameOperations is never refreshed, and Write-PendingFileRenameAdvisory is never called. No advisory line is emitted, and the diagnostics manifest reports PendingFileCleanup as unknown - see -h2z0 and ADR-0004.

This is the worst of the four absence causes because it is anti-correlated with quietness: it fires precisely when real servicing happened, which is when the pending-file evidence is most worth capturing. A reboot is about to occur, and the bundle records nothing about what was queued to be deleted across it.

The short-circuit itself is correct and must stay: the comment at :2505 explains that explicit 3010/1641 evidence is durable for the process and deliberately bypasses the settle-and-recheck wait, so it should not be made to pay for two probes plus a 20-second settle. The defect is that bypassing the WAIT also bypasses the RECORDING.

Likely shape of the fix: on the explicit-request path, still capture and record pending-file state (from the last known operations, or a cheap non-settling probe) before returning, marking the record as taken on the explicit-reboot path so a reader can see it did not come from a full two-probe confirmation. Do not introduce a settle wait on this path.

Filed separately from -h2z0 because this changes control flow in Get-ConfirmedPendingReboot, which is reboot-lifecycle logic. Needs /reboot-resilience-review and the test gates, not just a diagnostics-export review. -h2z0 covers the three purely-reporting causes (empty set, duplicate suppression, phase skipped).
acceptance_criteria: The explicit-reboot path in Get-ConfirmedPendingReboot records pending-file cleanup state before returning; the record is marked as taken on the explicit-reboot path so a reader can distinguish it from a full two-probe confirmation; no settle wait is introduced on that path and the existing 3010/1641 bypass of the settle-and-recheck delay is preserved; a run in which an installer returns 3010 produces a diagnostics manifest with a determinate BeforeMutationState rather than not-probed; covered by tests/RebootResilience.Tests.ps1 and reviewed under /reboot-resilience-review with the test gates.
close_reason: Fixed. Get-ConfirmedPendingReboot still short-circuits on an explicit 3010/1641 request and still bypasses the settle-and-recheck wait - that behaviour is correct and is now pinned by a test asserting zero settle waits and zero Test-PendingReboot calls on that path - but it no longer bypasses the recording. The Session Manager read was extracted into Update-BootUpdatePendingFileRenameSnapshot so the explicit path can refresh the snapshot with one registry read, and the resulting record is marked Source=explicit-reboot so a reader can distinguish it from a full two-probe confirmation. Evidence: four new tests in tests/RebootResilience.Tests.ps1, Describe 'An explicit 3010 records pending-file state instead of skipping it' - the record is written with observation observed-nonempty and the queued fingerprint before the explicit request is returned, it is marked explicit-reboot, no settle wait or second probe is introduced, and a run with no explicit request still does the full two-probe confirmation. Invoke-Pester tests/RebootResilience.Tests.ps1 = 250 passed / 0 failed. Reviewed against the reboot-resilience checklist; the full test gates run at the end of Phase 1. Commit fa1bf87.

title: [bug] Diagnostics manifest infers pending-cleanup state from the absence of a log line
description:
The diagnostics manifest infers machine state from the non-appearance of a log line. See ADR-0004 ("Absence of a record is not a record of absence") and the CONTEXT.md term "negative evidence".

OBSERVED. Bundle 20260825-130554Z, session 2026-08-25 08:20:56, v2.5.76, a completed and converged run: PendingFileCleanup.BeforeMutation=null and Persistent=null. The truthful answer is Persistent=false. The two ApplicationCleanup entries (5F8FDB30BE01, 8956A7C22992) were created by that cycle's own Chocolatey upgrade of PowerToys 0.100.2 to 0.101.2362, and cleared on the next reboot.

ROOT CAUSE. Get-BootUpdateDiagnosticCleanupSummary (Export-BootUpdateDiagnostics.ps1, approx. 210-219) derives the pre-mutation state solely from whether a "Pending-file cleanup [before mutation]" line is present:

    $before = if ($contexts.Contains('before mutation')) { ... } else { $null }
    if ($before -and $after) { $persistent = ... }   # otherwise stays $null

Write-PendingFileRenameAdvisory (Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:2420) declines to emit that line for FOUR unrelated reasons, all of which collapse to the same null:

  1. Empty advisory set - early return at :2426.
  2. Duplicate suppression - the $script:LastPendingFileCleanupFingerprint guard at :2428 returns when the same context+fingerprint was already logged. Get-ConfirmedPendingReboot deliberately calls the advisory twice (:2515, :2523), once per probe.
  3. Explicit-reboot short-circuit - Get-ConfirmedPendingReboot returns $script:ExplicitRebootRequests at :2510 BEFORE reaching the advisory, so on any 3010/1641 the pending-file state is never probed. Tracked separately; this is reboot-lifecycle behaviour, not reporting.
  4. Phase never ran - the after-updates call at :7224 is -WhatIf gated; the before-mutation call at :6494 is not.

THIS BEAD covers causes 1, 2 and 4. Cause 3 is a separate bead because it changes an early return in Get-ConfirmedPendingReboot and needs a reboot-resilience review rather than a diagnostics review.

DESIGN (settled 2026-08-28).

Emit a BootUpdateCycle.pending-cleanup.json sidecar and have the exporter prefer it, falling back to log-parsing so the ~197 historical log pairs still resolve.

The sidecar is on an EVIDENCE lifecycle, not a cache lifecycle. Do not model it on BootUpdateCycle.wu-assessment.json: that file looks like the obvious precedent but is a TTL'd cache (Set-WindowsUpdateAssessmentCache :3657 skips under $WhatIfPreference; Test-WindowsUpdateAssessmentRecord :3728 invalidates on age/scope/fingerprint; Remove-WindowsUpdateAssessmentCache deletes it). Copying that lifecycle reproduces cause 4. Model it on BootUpdateCycle-repair-plan.txt and BootUpdateCycle-winget-quarantine.json instead: written to be read later, never expired. Add it to the exporter allowlist at Export-BootUpdateDiagnostics.ps1:274.

Records are per pass, appended, keyed by session id and pass number - not a single overwritten snapshot. Whether a fingerprint survived a restart is only answerable across passes, which is the open question in -2bx.

Recording and display separate. The duplicate guard at :2428 STAYS - suppressing repeat probe lines in the log is legitimate - but it stops carrying evidentiary weight, because the log is no longer the evidence. Record every observation in the sidecar with its probe index.

Manifest shape: Persistent stays a plain boolean wherever determinable, and a sibling BeforeMutationState carries the nuance, with values observed-empty, observed-nonempty, suppressed-duplicate, not-probed, phase-skipped, unknown-legacy-log. Bundles predating this change report unknown-legacy-log with Persistent=null, so a historical limitation stays distinguishable from a current-format bundle that failed to record.

WHY IT MATTERS. The manifest is release evidence for the truthful-convergence claim in ADR-0003. "New, self-inflicted, clears on reboot" and "unknown" are materially different stories and the bundle currently cannot tell them apart. Note also that Write-Log (:850) writes to file unconditionally and Visibility gates only the console, so this is NOT output-mode-dependent - that was checked and ruled out.

RELATED. -vla0 is the same defect class in a different field (Phase="s ran"). A follow-up bead covers the general evidence.json that would retire log-parsing for all machine-readable manifest fields; ADR-0004 records why that is the destination but not this step.
acceptance_criteria: Pending-cleanup evidence is recorded to a BootUpdateCycle.pending-cleanup.json sidecar on an evidence lifecycle (no TTL, no fingerprint invalidation, not skipped under -WhatIf) and added to the exporter allowlist; records are appended per pass keyed by session id and pass number, each carrying its probe index; the duplicate-suppression guard in Write-PendingFileRenameAdvisory is retained for the log but no longer determines what is recorded; the manifest exposes Persistent as a plain boolean wherever determinable plus a BeforeMutationState sibling with values observed-empty, observed-nonempty, suppressed-duplicate, not-probed, phase-skipped, unknown-legacy-log; the exporter prefers the sidecar and falls back to log-parsing for pre-change bundles, which report unknown-legacy-log with Persistent null; Persistent is false (not null) for the 2026-08-25 08:20:56 case where the before-state was observed and empty while the after-state was non-empty; regression tests in tests/DiagnosticsExport.Tests.ps1 cover observed-empty, suppressed-duplicate, phase-skipped, unchanged-non-empty, and legacy-log bundles.
close_reason: Implemented as designed. The cycle writes BootUpdateCycle.pending-cleanup.json beside the state file, on the evidence lifecycle ADR-0004 describes: no TTL, no fingerprint invalidation, written under -WhatIf, appended per probe, keyed by session id (the run's StartTime) and pass, each record carrying its probe index, context, observation, source, categories and fingerprints; capped by count at 500, never by age. Write-PendingFileRenameAdvisory now records first and unconditionally - observed-empty, observed-nonempty or suppressed-duplicate - and the duplicate guard is retained for the log only. The -WhatIf after-updates skip records phase-skipped rather than leaving the same silence. Export-BootUpdateDiagnostics collects the sidecar (added to the allowlist), prefers it, and derives BeforeMutation, AfterUpdates, Persistent and a new BeforeMutationState sibling from it, grouping by session so one run's before-state is never compared with another's after-state; bundles with no sidecar fall back to log parsing and report BeforeMutationState unknown-legacy-log instead of a bare null. Evidence: Invoke-Pester tests/DiagnosticsExport.Tests.ps1 = 21 passed / 0 failed, including the 2026-08-25 case (before observed-empty, after observed-nonempty) now returning Persistent false rather than null, plus unchanged-non-empty true, suppressed-duplicate, phase-skipped, not-probed, cross-session isolation, and the legacy fallback; Invoke-Pester tests/RebootResilience.Tests.ps1 = 250 passed / 0 failed, including six behavioural tests that every probe is recorded whatever the log does. Not yet observed in a real bundle from a lab guest; that comes with the v2.5.79 validation rows, and -5vbd stays deferred until it has been. Commit fa1bf87.

title: Chocolatey: repeated identical package checksum failure is treated as retryable
description:
choco upgrade all fails deterministically on a single package whose published checksum no longer matches the artifact the vendor is serving. The updater classifies this as a retryable partial failure, so the phase never completes and the cycle keeps queuing recovery passes.

Observed with GoogleChrome on 2026-08-24:
  You have GoogleChrome v152.0.7977.42 installed. Version <redacted> is available based on your source(s).
  Error - hashes do not match. Actual value was 'B5F03C8D...'
  Download of googlechromestandaloneenterprise64.msi (-1 B) completed.
  Error - hashes do not match. Actual value was 'B5F03C8D...'
  ERROR: Checksum for '<path>'
  The upgrade of GoogleChrome was NOT successful.
  Chocolatey upgraded 0/14 packages. 1 packages failed.
  Failures
   - GoogleChrome (exited -1)

Note the retry inside Chocolatey itself: it re-downloads from the vendor and gets the same actual hash both times. This is an upstream package-metadata defect. The failure is fully deterministic and no number of passes will resolve it.

Updater response each pass:
  [Warn] Updating Chocolatey packages: child process exited with code -1.
  [Error] Chocolatey upgrade failed or timed out; retry required.
  [Warn] Chocolatey: 0 package(s) updated (partial failure).
  [Error] <<< [2/10] Chocolatey - FAILED (0.5 min, 0 pkg)
  [Warn] Verification withheld: incomplete phase(s): Chocolatey. Automatic retry queued for two minutes.

Current behaviour: the boot-session round-trip bug was masking the blast radius. With the retry budget resetting every pass, this looped indefinitely (42 passes in one session). Now that MaxRetryPasses is reachable, the cycle stops after 5 passes and escalates to manual attention. That is a correct floor, but it still spends five full Chocolatey passes re-attempting a download that cannot succeed.

Proposal: treat a repeated identical package-level failure signature as terminal rather than retryable, and escalate to Attention on the second occurrence instead of exhausting the budget. Winget already has this shape (WingetFailureSignature / WingetFailureRepeatCount, with Complete-WingetFailureClassification and Invoke-WingetFailureQuarantine); Chocolatey has no equivalent. A checksum mismatch reporting the same actual hash across passes is about as clean a terminal signature as exists.

Worth considering whether the escalation should quarantine just the offending package and let the rest of the phase verify, rather than failing the whole phase: 13 of 14 packages were already current in the run above.

Not reproducible on demand; it clears whenever the package maintainer refreshes the checksum. Captured provider output is in the 2026-08-24 diagnostics bundle.

Mirrored to GitHub as nanoDBA/boot-upd#51 while bd was unreachable.
close_reason: Escalation shipped in v2.5.75 (0cdb757, 7dee570). Repeated identical Chocolatey failures now classify as terminal at repeat>=2 and route to manual attention with a repair plan, instead of consuming the full retry budget. Validated in production 2026-08-24: stopped at pass 2 with both hashes in the plan and no bypass command. Quarantining the offending package so the rest of the phase can converge was scoped out and is tracked separately.

title: [P2] Per-package Winget exit-code reconciliation ignores non-aggregate stale-record codes
description:
## Problem

Diagnostics from 2026-08-24 show a recurring contradiction in the Winget phase log, once per run,
for a package with a stale/incomplete uninstall record:

```
[Warn] [STALE] Microsoft.WindowsPCHealthCheck is already absent, but Winget retains an incomplete uninstall record.
[Warn] [OK] This stale record will not fail the update run or trigger another automatic pass.
[Info] Winget machine/Microsoft.WindowsPCHealthCheck: 0 attempted, 0 updated, 0 failed, 1 stale record(s) need attention.
[Error] Winget (machine/Microsoft.WindowsPCHealthCheck) returned -1978335184 (0x8A150030); partial failure, retry required.
```

The "[OK] ... will not fail the update run or trigger another automatic pass" message is
immediately contradicted by the "[Error] ... partial failure, retry required" line two lines later,
on every affected run (seen repeatedly through 2026-08, still current on v2.5.72).

## Root cause

`Test-WingetExitReconciled` (Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:1101-1118) only reconciles the aggregate
bulk-upgrade exit code `0x8A15002C` (-1978335188). Per-package targeted upgrades
(Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:3019, `Write-WingetScopeSummary -Scope "$scope/$pkgId" ...`) return
their own distinct per-package exit code -- observed here as `0x8A150030` (-1978335184) -- which is
never in the reconciliation allowlist. The unconditional exit-code check at line 1474-1475 then
logs it as an `[Error]` "partial failure, retry required" even though the structured output for
that same package was fully accounted for as a stale/absent record one line above.

This contradicts the documented rule in .claude/rules/powershell-updater-safety.md: "Never count
1605, a provider trigger, or an inferred action as a verified update. Do not queue a retry for a
fully reconciled stale record." It does not appear to flip the phase to FAILED by itself (that is
driven by `$script:CurrentWingetFailures`/`$anyTimeout`), but it is misleading Error-level log
noise on every affected run and undermines diagnostics truthfulness.

## Acceptance criteria

- `Test-WingetExitReconciled` (or an equivalent per-package-aware check) recognizes per-package
  exit codes that are fully accounted for by that single package'"'"'s own stale/scope-blocked/deferred
  classification, not just the one hardcoded aggregate code.
- The "[OK] ... will not fail the update run" message and the exit-code-derived Error log line
  never contradict each other for the same package outcome.
- Pester coverage: a per-package stale-record fixture with exit code 0x8A150030 (and the aggregate
  0x8A15002C case) must not produce the contradictory Error line.
- `./tools/Invoke-TestGates.ps1` passes.
close_reason: Fixed in commit (pending); Test-WingetExitReconciled generalized from one hardcoded aggregate exit code to any non-success code once structured output fully accounts for it. Pester 307/307, cross-context-mutex, and published-launcher-upgrade gates pass.

title: [P2] Stop diagnostics IP redaction from erasing dotted package versions
description:
## Problem

The supplied sanitized logs replace dotted package versions with `<IP>` in Winget tables. The current sanitizer treats every four-component dotted numeric token as an IPv4 address, so valid versions such as four-part application/build versions lose the installed/available evidence needed to diagnose convergence.

## Diagnostics impact

- Installed and target versions cannot be compared.
- Changed-evidence and stale-inventory analysis becomes ambiguous.
- Support bundles lose non-sensitive package metadata while still retaining unrelated surrounding text.

## Acceptance criteria

- Valid IPv4 addresses remain redacted.
- Dotted package/file/product versions in known structured provider output remain available, or are replaced with a distinct stable version placeholder that preserves equality/change relationships.
- Ambiguous tokens use a documented privacy-first rule with contextual parsing rather than unconditional global replacement.
- Tests cover private/public IPv4 addresses, four-part versions, versions adjacent to package IDs, and ordinary prose.
- The post-sanitization assertion continues to reject real IP leakage.
- Existing identity, path, URL, email, SID, GUID, MAC, UNC, and registry redaction behavior is unchanged.

title: [P2] Export diagnostics from a consistent snapshot and mark active runs
description:
## Problem

The 2026-08-15 10:40Z bundle was exported while the active cycle was still running and ends mid-Windows-Update phase. Eight minutes later, the 10:48Z bundle contains the completed outcome. The format-v1 manifest only records generation time, source count, sanitization, and a hash; it does not say that an active log was captured mid-run or identify the source snapshots.

Because files are read directly while writers may still append, an export can represent an arbitrary cut without enough metadata to distinguish “cycle still active” from “log truncated/cycle crashed.”

## Acceptance criteria

- Export reads each source from a stable snapshot (copy/open-sharing strategy documented and tested).
- Manifest format is versioned forward and records sanitized source name, captured length, last-write time, and hash per source.
- Manifest records whether the cycle/state indicated an active run at capture time and, when available, its phase/iteration without exposing identity or paths.
- A support reader can distinguish completed, active-at-capture, and unexpectedly truncated diagnostics.
- Export remains safe when the active log is locked or appended during capture; failures are explicit and do not produce a misleading “complete” bundle.
- Tests simulate concurrent append during export and verify internally consistent hashes/lengths.

title: [P2] Preserve source-log encoding during sanitized diagnostics export
description:
## Problem

All three supplied sanitized bundles contain mojibake in provider output (for example a Unicode ellipsis rendered as `ΓÇª`). The exporter is compatible with Windows PowerShell 5.1 and reads each source via `Get-Content -Raw` without an explicit or detected encoding, then writes UTF-8. A UTF-8 source without a BOM is therefore liable to be decoded using the legacy Windows PowerShell default before export.

## Diagnostics impact

Corrupted punctuation and non-ASCII package/provider text makes table parsing evidence harder to interpret and can alter identifiers or localized messages.

## Acceptance criteria

- UTF-8 source logs with and without BOM round-trip into the sanitized bundle without mojibake.
- UTF-16LE/BOM logs remain supported if they are valid inputs.
- Invalid byte sequences are surfaced in the manifest or exporter warning rather than silently replaced.
- Sanitization still runs on decoded text and all existing privacy assertions remain enforced.
- Tests include UTF-8 no-BOM provider output with ellipsis and representative non-ASCII package text.
- The resulting consolidated log is UTF-8 with a documented BOM policy.

title: Investigate repeating FileRename reboot signal across reboots
description: Diagnostics 2026-07-24: three occurrences of 'Same reboot-signal set as the previous reboot (FileRename)' in the 2026-07-20 session (17:14, 17:24, 19:16). The log's own guidance says a repeating set is likely a stale or perpetually repopulated signal. Identify which PendingFileRenameOperations entries persist across reboots and whether they should be filtered as routine (cf. 'ApplicationCleanup=4, delete-only housekeeping' pending-file cleanup lines) before counting toward reboot decisions.
notes:
2026-08-25 diagnostics (bundle 20260825-130554Z): the three ApplicationCleanup fingerprints 1B12D6006E07/1D50219B2C6C/660332112DBC seen persisting across the 06:05 and 06:25 runs did NOT survive the reboot at boot session 2026-08-25T12:13:43Z. They cleared; the two entries in the 08:20 run (5F8FDB30BE01, 8956A7C22992) are new and were created by that cycle's own PowerToys upgrade. So far no evidence of a rename entry surviving a reboot. See -h2z0 for the separate manifest-fidelity gap that made this harder to read.
2026-08-28 (grill session, ADR-0004). Two things this investigation now depends on.

First, the 2026-08-25 evidence: the three ApplicationCleanup fingerprints seen across the 06:05 and 06:25 runs did NOT survive the reboot at boot session 2026-08-25T12:13:43Z. They cleared, and the two entries in the 08:20 run were new, created by that cycle's own PowerToys upgrade. Still no observed case of a rename entry surviving a restart.

Second, and the reason this bead is hard to close: that conclusion cannot be reached from a single diagnostics bundle. It required hand-diffing two bundles captured three days apart, because the manifest holds one overwritten snapshot rather than per-pass records. -h2z0 now specifies pending-cleanup records appended per pass and keyed by session id and pass number, which is exactly the shape that would make "did this fingerprint survive a restart" answerable from one bundle. Treat -h2z0 as a practical prerequisite for closing this.
2026-09-08 (bundle 20260908-123444Z, run of 2026-09-07 08:33). FIRST CONFIRMED CASE of rename entries surviving reboots. This overturns the standing "no evidence" conclusion in the two notes above.

Fingerprints 5BF18DDAD3F6, F2377C60A334, FF7D58BFCE6B, category PackageManagementPrototypeCleanup (NOT ApplicationCleanup, which is what the earlier investigation tracked).

First sighting 2026-07-24 14:01 before-mutation (5BF18DDAD3F6; the other two by 14:17 after-updates). Still present 2026-09-07 08:36 after-updates, and confirmed live in the registry by hand at 08:37:25. That is 45 days.

The discriminator the 2026-08-28 note asked for is now available without hand-diffing bundles, because the surrounding set churns hard while these three do not. Before-mutation counts over the history: 6, 6, 1, 2, 3, 6, 6, 6, 6, 6, 36, 9, 24, 3. Critically, on 2026-09-06 13:32 the value held dozens of entries with a completely different fingerprint set (001365EDC914, 00338055A20D, 01328A200BC4, ...), and by 2026-09-07 07:54 the value held exactly these three and nothing else. PendingFileRenameOperations is consumed only by smss at boot, so a boot occurred in that window, processed and cleared every sibling entry, and left these three.

So these three are either never consumed or perfectly repopulated. Either way the operational consequence is real and not cosmetic: any naive pending-reboot check on this machine is permanently positive. The 4sysops-style test (any non-null PendingFileRenameOperations means pending reboot) reports Pending forever, which will mislead SCCM, Ansible, and any deployment tooling that uses that pattern. The updater itself is correct and unaffected; it classifies these as delete-only housekeeping and says no restart is required.

Hypothesis to test: the legacy PackageManagement/OneGet Chocolatey provider re-extracts C:\Windows\SystemTemp\ChocolateyPrototype-2.8.5.130\<n> and re-registers the delete whenever it initializes. Identical paths yield identical fingerprints, which fits the evidence exactly. CLAUDE.md already warns that broad Get-Package/Find-Package/provider-discovery probes can bootstrap legacy providers.

Decisive next experiment, cheap and needs no code: after the next reboot, read PendingFileRenameOperations BEFORE running any update cycle. If the three are already present, something at boot re-creates them. If absent, they are re-created during the run, and the next question is by which phase. Do not rewrite the registry value to clear them; that is forbidden per the updater-safety rule and would destroy the evidence.

description: Exercise two or more real reboot/resume transitions, canceled shutdown watchdog behavior, user-primary plus SYSTEM-fallback tasks, delayed registry evidence, and terminal cleanup on a disposable Windows VM.
notes:
Capture environment inventory: local Windows 11 Home has no Hyper-V, Sandbox, VirtualBox, or VMware. omada-debian exposes /dev/kvm and ample disk but only ~4.6 GiB available RAM while running production containers, with no QEMU/libvirt installed. The same-boot retry half of this gate is now evidenced on real hardware; the multi-reboot half is not.

v2.5.73 (before d737376): "Observed a new Windows boot session" fired on every retry pass with no reboot between (212 occurrences overall; last at 12:20:57). ConsecutiveRetryCount was zeroed each reload, so the recovery limit was unreachable and a permanently failing Chocolatey phase ran 42 passes / 358.4 min on 08-22.

The 13:47-13:59 retry chain ran 4 passes and terminated correctly with "Same-boot recovery limit 5 reached; incomplete phases: Chocolatey. Continuation tasks were removed and verified absent." Still owed by this gate and NOT covered by the above: two or more REAL reboots, canceled delayed restart, failed restart command, delayed reboot signal, SYSTEM-fallback continuation with no user logged on, and the OS/PowerShell matrix. Every pass in the evidence above was same-boot with 0 reboots.
2026-09-08. ENVIRONMENT NOTE ABOVE IS NOW STALE AND MISLEADING. It says "local Windows 11 Home has no Hyper-V, Sandbox, VirtualBox, or VMware" and points at provisioning an isolated runner. This machine (the maintainer workstation) is Windows 11 PRO, and a working disposable lab now exists locally. Do not go provision cloud infrastructure for this gate.

Lab as built:
- Hyper-V enabled (required one host restart). 253GB free, 23.7GB RAM, 8 logical CPUs, VT-x already active for VBS.
- Guest: boot-upd-matrix. Gen 2, vTPM + Secure Boot on, 4 vCPU, 4-8GB dynamic, 60GB dynamic VHDX, Default Switch (NAT internet verified: DNS resolves, HTTPS 200, wuauserv running).
- OS: Windows 11 Enterprise LTSC 2024 Evaluation, build 26100, installed unattended from C:\HyperV\unattend\autounattend.xml. Local admin "updtest", auto-logon with no expiry counter. Verified across a real reboot: Win32_ComputerSystem.UserName = UPDTESTVM\updtest with nobody at the keyboard.
- Media and scripts under C:\HyperV. Build script C:\HyperV\New-BootUpdTestVm.ps1.

Checkpoints (Standard, so memory state is captured and a revert resumes mid-run):
  baseline-clean     PS 5.1 only, auto-logon ON      -> PS5.1 bootstrap rows
  |- ps7-installed   + PowerShell 7.6.5              -> existing-PS7 rows
  |- no-autologon    auto-logon OFF, nobody signed in -> SYSTEM-fallback row
Revert measured at 7.5s and proven non-trivial: a sentinel file and registry key written before the revert were both gone after, while the baseline marker survived and the auto-logon session came back. Reverting to baseline-clean also removes PS7, so the branches are genuinely independent.

Still to build: updater-deployed (from ps7-installed) once upd is on the guest.

TRAP FOUND, applies to every scenario in this gate: do NOT use Restart-VM to drive guest reboots. It is a hard reset. A registry write and a file write made immediately before one were both silently lost, because the hive and file buffers had not flushed. In a gate whose whole subject is checkpoint state surviving restarts, that would produce false updater failures. Drive reboots with shutdown /r inside the guest, and reserve the hard reset for a scenario that is deliberately simulating power loss.

Two known gaps, neither blocking the reboot rows: LTSC ships without the Store so winget is absent (App Installer must be layered on deliberately for provider-coverage rows), and the build script still boots the installer ISO, which needs a keypress at "Press any key to boot from CD or DVD" (currently worked around by driving Msvm_Keyboard). Converting the build to apply install.wim with DISM + bcdboot would make rebuilds genuinely unattended.
2026-09-08. Checkpoint tree rebuilt COLD. The original Standard (running-state) checkpoints were unusable and the reason is worth recording, because it will bite anyone who builds this lab the obvious way.

A Standard checkpoint captures live RAM. Restoring one resumes a session that still believes it is the wall-clock time of capture, so Windows locks the workstation and replays logon overlays. Consecutive probes of the same restored guest saw explorer running one moment and LogonUI the next. The console state after such a restore is non-deterministic, which is useless as a test baseline and cost real time chasing phantom boot failures.

Worse, the originals were taken without ever looking at the console, only at PowerShell Direct. One captured a machine still sitting on an OOBE "Just a moment, checking for updates" screen. PowerShell Direct answers perfectly happily in that state.

SEPARATE ROOT CAUSE, and the one that actually stranded the guest at a logon prompt repeatedly: Windows DELETES AutoAdminLogon, DefaultUserName and DefaultPassword from Winlogon after consuming an autologon. Verified empirically - all three read null after the first successful autologon. So autologon configured once is a one-shot, not a property. Mitigation: C:\Lab\Repair-AutoLogon.ps1 plus scheduled task Lab-RepairAutoLogon (SYSTEM, at startup) re-asserts all four values and strips AutoLogonCount every boot. Proven across two consecutive reboots, both reaching a desktop with AutoAdminLogon back to 1.

Current tree, both taken with the VM OFF so every restore is an identical cold boot:
  staged                 PS7 7.6.5 + working tree at C:\Lab\boot-upd + autologon repair task
  |- staged-no-autologon autologon off AND Lab-RepairAutoLogon DISABLED (or it re-enables at boot)

Verified by restoring each, booting, and capturing the console:
  staged              -> Off, boot, autologon desktop in 44s (explorer 1, LogonUI 0)
  staged-no-autologon -> Off, boot, logon screen (user empty, explorer 0, LogonUI 1)

Cost of a cold reset is ~45-60s versus 7.5s for the running-state kind. Worth every second for determinism.

Rows still needing a checkpoint that no longer exists: F (PS5.1-only bootstrap) needs a guest without PowerShell 7. Deleting the old checkpoints merged their state into the base disk, so baseline-clean and ps7-installed are gone. Row F needs either a PS7 uninstall on a throwaway branch or a fresh guest.

title: Reboot fails when machine is locked (error 1271 - missing /f flag)
description:
## Bug

When the machine is locked at the time the script attempts to reboot, `shutdown.exe` fails with error 1271:

```
The machine is locked and cannot be shut down without the force option.(1271)
```

This leaves the cycle stuck — updates completed, scheduled task registered, but no reboot happens.

## Root cause

`Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1` line 1017 calls:

```powershell
& shutdown.exe /r /t $script:RebootDelaySec /c $shutdownComment /d p:2:17
```

The `/f` (force) flag is missing. Windows requires `/f` to restart a locked machine.

## Expected behavior

The script should force the restart since it's an automated update cycle. The user already had the opportunity to cancel via the reboot warning / `shutdown /a`.

## Suggested fix

Add `/f` to the shutdown command:

```powershell
& shutdown.exe /r /f /t $script:RebootDelaySec /c $shutdownComment /d p:2:17
```

## Log excerpt

```
[2026-04-25 15:30:37] [Info] Initiating shutdown /r /t 0 | Cancel: shutdown /a
The machine is locked and cannot be shut down without the force option.(1271)
[2026-04-25 15:30:37] [Info] Shutdown scheduled. Exiting; will resume after reboot.
```

Note: the script logs "Shutdown scheduled" even though shutdown.exe failed — exit code is not checked.

## Secondary issue

The script does not check the exit code of `shutdown.exe`, so it reports success and exits even when the reboot was never initiated.

title: Bug: BBS splash renders blank on Server 2016 / older conhost (encoding)
description:
## Symptom

When launched via ``upd.cmd`` on Windows Server 2016, the ``Show-StartupArt`` BBS splash renders as empty lines. The lean cyan ``Show-CycleBanner`` (using ASCII ``=``/``-``) renders fine; only the Unicode-heavy splash is affected.

## Root Cause

cmd.exe defaults to OEM/ANSI code page (CP437 or CP1252). When ``pwsh`` is launched as a child, ``[Console]::OutputEncoding`` inherits that code page (verified: ``ibm437``). Block-drawing chars (``█`` U+2588, ``╗`` U+2557, ``═`` U+2550, ``░▒▓`` U+2591-2593) get stripped on output.

## Fix

Force UTF-8 console I/O at the top of ``Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1``:

- ``[Console]::OutputEncoding = UTF8``
- ``[Console]::InputEncoding = UTF8``
- ``chcp 65001``

Wrapped in ``try/catch`` so SYSTEM scheduled-task runs (no console attached) don't error.

Tested on Windows Server 2016.

title: Enhancement: Migrate module updates to PSResourceGet with bulk Update-PSResource
description:
## Description

Replace the sequential `Start-Job { Update-Module }` loop (139 modules × 5min timeout each) with `Update-PSResource -Name *` for a single bulk update call. PSResourceGet is C#-native, ~2x faster, and eliminates PackageManagement dependency conflicts.

## Current Implementation

```powershell
foreach ($mod in $modules) {
    $job = Start-Job { Update-Module -Name $modName -Force }
    Wait-Job -Timeout ($perModTimeout * 60)
    # ... per-module error handling
}
```

**Problems:** 139 sequential gallery round-trips, Start-Job spawns full pwsh.exe per module (~200-500ms overhead each), PackageManagement conflicts, orphan processes on timeout.

## Proposed Implementation

```powershell
# Prefer PSResourceGet (bundled with PS 7.4+)
if (Get-Command Update-PSResource -EA SilentlyContinue) {
    $job = Start-Job {
        Update-PSResource -Name * -Scope AllUsers -Force -AcceptLicense `
            -TrustRepository -Quiet -PassThru 2>&1
    }
    $done = $job | Wait-Job -Timeout (30 * 60)  # Single 30min timeout for all
    # ... handle results
} else {
    # Fallback: existing per-module Update-Module logic
}
```

## Key Benefits

- **Single call** replaces 139 sequential round-trips
- **Child process** avoids module-in-use file locks
- **Dependency-aware** — handles AWS.Tools.Common → AWS.Tools.* ordering automatically
- **No PackageManagement** — PSResourceGet bypasses it entirely
- **2x faster** in benchmarks

## Research Sources

- PSResourceGet GA since Oct 2023, current stable **1.1.1** (March 2025)
- Friedrich Weinmann PSConfEU 2025: "Package Management: The Way We Always Wanted It To Be"
- Jeff Hicks recommends migration in "PowerShell Refresh" blog post
- JustinGrote's optimized version-check gist for pre-filtering
- PSGallery rate limits at ~10-20 concurrent API calls; `Update-PSResource -Name *` serializes internally

## Considerations

- Requires `Microsoft.PowerShell.PSResourceGet` 1.1.1+ (bundled with PS 7.4+)
- Old module versions are installed side-by-side (not removed) — may want cleanup phase
- `AWS.Tools.*` should use `Update-AWSToolsModule -CleanUp` from `AWS.Tools.Installer`
- Keep fallback to `Update-Module` for PS 7.0-7.3 compatibility

title: Enhancement: Webhook notification retry on transient failure
description:
## Description

Webhook notifications (`Invoke-RestMethod`) have no retry logic. If the POST fails due to a transient network error (timeout, 503, DNS hiccup), the notification is silently lost.

```powershell
$response = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri $url -Method Post -Body $jsonBody `
    -ContentType 'application/json' -TimeoutSec 10 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
```

## Suggested Fix

Add simple retry with backoff (e.g., 3 attempts with 2/4/8 second delays). Keep fail-forward behavior — exhausted retries should log a warning but never abort the cycle.

## Severity

LOW — notifications are informational. The cycle completes regardless. History and event log provide alternative audit trails.

title: Bug: Stop-Job doesn't kill child pwsh process for module updates
description:
## Description

PowerShell module updates use `Start-Job` with `Wait-Job -Timeout`. When a module update times out, `Stop-Job` is called, but this only stops the PowerShell job — the underlying child `pwsh.exe` process may continue running as an orphan.

```powershell
$job = Start-Job -ScriptBlock { param($N) Update-Module -Name $N -Force -EA Stop 2>&1 } -ArgumentList $modName
$done = $job | Wait-Job -Timeout ($perModTimeout * 60)
if (-not $done) {
    $job | Stop-Job -PassThru | Remove-Job -Force  # Job stops, but child process may survive
}
```

## Suggested Fix

After `Stop-Job`, enumerate and kill child processes of the job's process:
```powershell
if (-not $done) {
    $childPid = $job.ChildJobs[0].Information[0]  # or track via ProcessId
    $job | Stop-Job -PassThru | Remove-Job -Force
    Get-Process -Id $childPid -EA SilentlyContinue | Stop-Process -Force
}
```

Or use the existing `Invoke-PackageManagerWithTimeout` function which has robust process tree management.

## Severity

MEDIUM — orphan processes consume resources but are cleaned up on next reboot. Only triggers when a module update hangs past the 5-minute per-module timeout.

```powershell
   Defer auth support to future iteration (SecretManagement/PSCredential). #>
```

## Suggested Approach

- Support `PSCredential` parameter for SMTP auth
- Optionally integrate with `SecretManagement` module for credential retrieval

## Severity

Additionally, if the URL contains PowerShell special characters, it could be misinterpreted when passed through scheduled task argument strings.

title: Bug: ExcludePatterns with special chars break scheduled task argument parsing
description:
## Description

Both `Deploy-BootUpdateCycle.ps1` (line 415) and `Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1` (line 1179) serialize ExcludePatterns for scheduled task arguments using simple single-quote wrapping:

```powershell
$patternStr = ($Config.ExcludePatterns | ForEach-Object { "'$_'" }) -join ','
$taskArgs += "-ExcludePatterns @($patternStr)"
```

If a pattern contains single quotes, commas, parentheses, dollar signs, or backticks, the command-line argument will be misinterpreted or fail to parse when the scheduled task invokes PowerShell.

**Examples that break:**
- `O'Reilly` → `-ExcludePatterns @('O'Reilly')` — unbalanced quotes
- `$(calc)` → potential command substitution
- `Test,Value` → PowerShell interprets as two array elements

## Suggested Fix

Use proper escaping (double single-quotes inside single-quoted strings) or serialize via JSON:
```powershell
$escapedPatterns = $Config.ExcludePatterns | ForEach-Object { $_ -replace "'", "''" }
```

## Severity

MEDIUM — only triggers with unusual characters in package name patterns. Common patterns like `Teams`, `OneDrive`, `SQL` are unaffected.

title: Bug: ExcludePatterns uses -like wildcard matching instead of substring
description:
## Description

`Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1` lines 705 and 780 use `-like "*$pattern*"` for ExcludePatterns matching. The `-like` operator treats `[]`, `?`, and `*` as wildcards.

**Example:** Pattern `Office[365]` matches `Office3`, `Office6`, `Office5` instead of the literal substring `Office[365]`.


## Fix

```powershell

```

title: Bug: Windows Update NotTitle parameter type error (array vs string)
description:
## Description

`Get-WindowsUpdate -NotTitle` is typed `[String]`, not `[String[]]`. The v2.1 ExcludePatterns integration passed an array (`@('SQL') + $script:ExcludePatterns`), causing:

```
Cannot convert 'System.Object[]' to the type 'System.String' required by parameter 'NotTitle'. Specified method is not supported.
```

## Root Cause

`Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1` line 819:
```powershell
NotTitle = (@('SQL') + $script:ExcludePatterns)  # Array, but -NotTitle expects String
```

## Fix

Join with `|` to produce a regex alternation string:
```powershell
NotTitle = ((@('SQL') + $script:ExcludePatterns) -join '|')
```

title: Bug: Repair-AwsTooling passes unsanitized UninstallString to cmd.exe
description:
## Description

`Repair-AwsTooling.ps1` reads the AWS CLI `UninstallString` from the registry and passes it directly to `cmd.exe /c` via string interpolation. A crafted registry entry containing shell metacharacters (`&`, `|`, etc.) would execute arbitrary commands.

## Impact

**Low in practice** — requires prior registry compromise, and the script already runs elevated. Flagging for defense-in-depth.

## Location

`Repair-AwsTooling.ps1` line 187:

```powershell
Start-Process cmd.exe -Wait -ArgumentList "/c $cmd"
```

## Suggested Fix

Use the MSI uninstall path directly rather than shelling out through `cmd.exe`, or validate the string matches expected MSI patterns before execution.

title: Bug: PowerShell module update jobs not validated for failure
description:
## Description

`Update-PowerShellModules` uses background jobs to update modules, but after `Receive-Job` it never checks `$job.State` for failures. A job that errors out is counted as success.

## Impact

**Medium** — Package counts in history/logs may overcount. No functional harm (modules just stay at current version), but misleading reporting.

## Location

`Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1` ~line 629:

```powershell
Receive-Job $job | ForEach-Object { Write-Log $_ }
Remove-Job $job -Force
```

## Suggested Fix

```powershell
$jobOutput = Receive-Job $job -EA SilentlyContinue
if ($jobOutput) { $jobOutput | ForEach-Object { Write-Log $_ } }
if ($job.State -eq 'Failed') {
    Write-Log "Module update job failed" -Level Warn
}
Remove-Job $job -Force
```

title: Bug: $LASTEXITCODE stale value causes false notification success logs
description:
## Description

The notification code checks `$LASTEXITCODE` after calling `msg.exe`, but `$LASTEXITCODE` may still hold a value from a previous external command. This can produce misleading log entries like "Notification: msg.exe sent" when it actually failed.

## Impact

**Low** — Cosmetic log inaccuracy only. Does not affect update behavior.

## Location

`Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1` ~line 775:

```powershell
if (Test-Path $msgExe) {
    & $msgExe * /TIME:120 "$Title`n`n$Message" 2>$null
    if ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 0) { Write-Log 'Notification: msg.exe sent' }
}
```

## Suggested Fix

Clear before use:

```powershell
$global:LASTEXITCODE = 0
& $msgExe * /TIME:120 "$Title`n`n$Message" 2>$null
if ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 0) { Write-Log 'Notification: msg.exe sent' }
else { Write-Log "msg.exe exited $LASTEXITCODE" -Level Warn }
```

title: Bug: crash recovery silently ignores unknown phase names
description:
## Description

When recovering from a crash (BSOD, power loss), the crash-recovery logic looks up `$State.LastPhaseStarted` in a `$phaseToFlag` hashtable. If the value is corrupted or unknown, the lookup returns `$null` and the code silently treats the phase as "not done" — no warning is logged.

## Impact

**Medium** — On state corruption, the script silently restarts from an unexpected point. Could lead to phases being re-run or skipped without any log trail explaining why.

## Location

`Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1` ~lines 238-239:

```powershell
$flagName = $phaseToFlag[$State.LastPhaseStarted]
$isDone = if ($flagName -and ($State.PSObject.Properties.Name -contains $flagName)) { [bool]$State.$flagName } else { $false }
```

## Suggested Fix

Log a warning when the phase name is unrecognized:

```powershell
if ($State.LastPhaseStarted -and -not $phaseToFlag.ContainsKey($State.LastPhaseStarted)) {
    Write-Log "WARNING: Unknown phase '$($State.LastPhaseStarted)' in crash recovery — resetting" -Level Warn
    $State.LastPhaseStarted = $null
}
```

title: Bug: pip JSON parsing breaks on single outdated package
description:
## Description

`Update-PipPackages` pipes `pip list --outdated --format=json` into `ConvertFrom-Json` without wrapping the result in `@()`. When exactly one package is outdated, `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a single PSObject instead of an array.

## Impact

**Medium** — `foreach` still works on a single object in PowerShell, so this doesn't crash. However, if pip returns malformed JSON or an error string, `ConvertFrom-Json -EA SilentlyContinue` returns `$null` and failures are silently swallowed with no log entry.

## Location

`Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1` ~line 584:

```powershell
$outdated = & pip list --outdated --format=json 2>$null | ConvertFrom-Json -EA SilentlyContinue
foreach ($pkg in $outdated) {
    Write-Log "Upgrading: $($pkg.name)"
    & pip install --upgrade $pkg.name 2>&1 | ForEach-Object { Write-Log $_ }
    $count++
}
```

## Suggested Fix

```powershell
$json = & pip list --outdated --format=json 2>$null
if (-not $json) { return @{ Success = $true; Count = 0 } }
$outdated = @($json | ConvertFrom-Json -EA SilentlyContinue)
if (-not $outdated) {
    Write-Log 'pip: failed to parse outdated list' -Level Warn
    return @{ Success = $true; Count = 0 }
}
```

title: Bug: $PID read-only variable collision crashes all package manager updates
description:
## Description

`Get-ProcessTreeActivity` in `Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1` uses `$pid` as a loop variable (line 387), which collides with PowerShell's read-only automatic variable `$PID` (current process ID). PowerShell variables are case-insensitive.

## Impact

**Critical** — Every package manager phase (winget, choco, etc.) crashes immediately on start with:

```
Cannot overwrite variable PID because it is read-only or constant.
```

The entire update cycle fails at phase 1.

## Root Cause

```powershell
# Line 387 — Get-ProcessTreeActivity BFS loop
$pid = $queue.Dequeue()   # $pid == $PID — read-only
```

## Fix

Rename `$pid` → `$procId` in the BFS loop.

## Status

**Fixed** in v2.0.1 (commit e2c64a8).

title: Investigate persistent PackageManagement cleanup requests across runs
description:
GitHub follow-up: #45

The updater has reported the same delete-only PackageManagementPrototypeCleanup fingerprints before and after completed runs. The behavior is treated as advisory and non-blocking: it does not by itself require a reboot or retry. A current large diagnostics bundle corroborates that the legacy cleanup entries recur, so this remains an unresolved investigation rather than a newly reproduced incident claim.

Determine why these legacy PackageManagement/OneGet cleanup requests remain in Windows pending-file state across completed runs, and document a safe remediation boundary. Do not rewrite the shared pending-file rename queue or force a reboot as part of diagnosis.

Acceptance criteria:

- Reproduce or explain persistence using a controlled fixture or sanitized evidence.
- Identify whether the entries are owned by an installed provider, stale registry state, or expected Windows servicing behavior.
- Define a reversible remediation, or explicitly document that no remediation is safe, including restart requirements.
- Add regression coverage so diagnostics distinguish persistent advisory cleanup from blocking reboot-required entries.

title: Lab: Hyper-V KVP status beacon from the guest
description: A guest-to-host heartbeat that needs no network and no credential. The guest publishes a few key/value pairs - cycle phase, pass number, reboot count, last log line - via the Hyper-V Data Exchange (KVP) service, and the host reads them over WMI (Msvm_KvpExchangeComponent / GuestExchangeItems). Two properties make this worth having over the existing PowerShell Direct poll: it stays readable in the windows where PowerShell Direct drops around a reboot, and it works before any credential is usable. Values are small, so this is a beacon, not a log shipper; the log stays in the guest and screenshots remain the fallback for console-only states. Explicitly NOT a guest-to-host network log shipper: that needs a listener or share, firewall rules and a credential to solve what VMBus already solves. Decide where the guest-side write lives: a tiny host-injected wrapper around the row is simplest; writing from the updater itself would make it a product feature and needs its own decision.
acceptance_criteria: With a row running, a host-side read of the guest's KVP items shows phase/pass/last-line updating, including during the interval where Invoke-Command -VMName fails because the guest is restarting. Nothing in the tracked updater code changes unless a separate decision says so.
notes: Deferred out of v2.5.79. The observability problem this was filed for is solved well enough for now by -35qb.6: host-timeline.txt is appended as each poll happens, so Get-Content -Wait on one or several guests is a live view that costs no agent tokens, and a killed row leaves its timeline behind. A KVP beacon would add guest-side status to that, which is a nice-to-have rather than something any v2.5.79 row needed.

title: A withheld phase is logged as a crash
description: When verification is withheld for an incomplete phase, the next pass logs 'Previous run crashed during [WindowsUpdate] at <time>. Restarting that phase.' Lab row B emitted this on every one of seven passes, which makes a healthy withhold-and-retry cycle read like repeated crashes to anyone reading the log or a diagnostics bundle. Distinguish the two intents in the message.

Test-CrashRecovery now reads the previous pass's terminal disposition off the state, which is still present when crash recovery runs, and distinguishes three histories that share one footprint: Phase RetryPending or UserContextPending logs 'Previous pass did not verify [<phase>] ... nothing crashed' at Info, Phase Rebooting logs 'Previous pass restarted Windows during [<phase>] ... nothing crashed' at Info, and anything else keeps the original 'Previous run crashed during [<phase>]' warning. The return value and therefore the behaviour - re-run the phase - is unchanged in all three cases. Evidence: five new tests in tests/RebootResilience.Tests.ps1, Describe 'A withheld phase is not reported as a crash', covering all three histories plus the finished-phase case that must log nothing; Invoke-Pester on that file is 240 passed / 0 failed. title: Process tree walk can attribute orphaned processes to a reused PID
description: Get-ProcessTreeActivity builds a parent-to-child map from Win32_Process without checking process creation time. Processes whose real parent has exited keep a stale ParentProcessId; if Windows reuses that PID for a package process, unrelated processes are counted into its tree.
design: Seen while verifying the UInt32/Int32 key fix: one sample reported ProcessCount=3 with 0.30s CPU for a target whose own CPU was 14.84s, i.e. the root was absent and strangers were attributed. Impact is limited now that an unobservable tree holds the idle clock rather than advancing it, so this inflates or misattributes a reading without causing a spurious kill. Fix would compare Win32_Process.CreationDate against the parent's before accepting an edge.
acceptance_criteria: Tree membership ignores edges where the claimed child started before the claimed parent.
close_reason: Fixed in the same change as the idle-detector repair (ADR-0005). Deferring was wrong: measurement showed a reused PID adopts orphans and can make a tree total FALL between samples (71 min of stranger CPU to 2s of real CPU). A falling total never exceeds the previous high-water mark, so the idle clock advances and kills working software - the exact spurious kill the parent fix addresses. Parent edges are now rejected when the claimed child predates the claimed parent, on both the measurement and the kill path.

title: Retire log-parsing as the source of machine-readable diagnostics manifest fields
description:
Retire log-parsing as the source of machine-readable manifest fields, replacing the per-field sidecars with one BootUpdateCycle.evidence.json covering pending-file cleanup, phase, and pass metadata.

ADR-0004 ("Absence of a record is not a record of absence") records this as the destination but deliberately not the first step: -h2z0 proves the artifact shape on the narrow pending-cleanup case first, and this bead generalises it once that shape has survived a release.

The manifest today reconstructs machine state by regex-matching prose written for humans (Export-BootUpdateDiagnostics.ps1:192, :203, and the Phase/Iteration matchers). Two filed defects are the same bug in different fields:

  -h2z0  PendingFileCleanup.Persistent collapses to null because the before-mutation line is absent, for any of four unrelated reasons.
  -vla0  Phase reported as "s ran" because the matcher struck the words "phase(s)" in the parallel-cohort banner, and Iteration came back null while the log plainly said Pass: 1.

Both exist because the log is doing double duty as a human narrative and a machine contract. Write-Log (:850) drops lines by more than a dozen pattern rules and collapses consecutive duplicates, so any wording change or new filter is a potential silent corruption of the manifest. That coupling is the thing to remove.

Scope: one evidence artifact on the evidence lifecycle described in ADR-0004 (never TTL'd, never skipped under -WhatIf, appended per pass and keyed by session id and pass number); exporter reads it in preference to any log parsing; log-parsing retained solely as the legacy path for bundles predating it, reporting explicit unknown-legacy-log states rather than bare nulls. Consider folding in the per-field sidecar from -h2z0 at that point rather than carrying both.

Blocked by -h2z0 in practice: do not start until the narrow artifact has shipped and been observed in a real bundle.
acceptance_criteria: A single BootUpdateCycle.evidence.json supplies every machine-readable manifest field (pending-file cleanup, phase, pass) on the ADR-0004 evidence lifecycle; the exporter derives no manifest field from log prose except for bundles predating the artifact; legacy bundles report explicit unknown-legacy-log states rather than bare nulls; -h2z0 and -vla0 are both closed or demonstrably subsumed; the per-field pending-cleanup sidecar is either folded in or its continued separate existence is justified in the ADR.

title: Chocolatey: quarantine a terminally failing package so the rest of the phase can converge
description:
Follow-up to #51, which shipped escalation only. When a Chocolatey package fails terminally, the whole phase fails, even though the other packages in the run may have verified. In the 2026-08-24 case 13 of 14 packages were already current and one had a broken checksum, yet the phase reported failure and the cycle stopped for manual attention.

Winget already has the machinery: `Invoke-WingetFailureQuarantine` places a reversible blocking pin, `Get-WingetQuarantineRecords` / `Set-WingetQuarantineRecords` persist the records to a durable sidecar merged with checkpoint state, and `upd uq <id>` lifts one. Chocolatey has no equivalent; `choco pin add -n=<package>` is the closest analogue.

## The decision this needs first

This is not simply "port the Winget code". It collides with the truthful-convergence invariant in `.claude/rules/powershell-updater-safety.md`, and the terms matter — see `CONTEXT.md`:

- **Quarantine** is an action taken against the package manager that persists until explicitly lifted.
- **Deferred** is recorded outstanding inventory: never a verified update, never retry fuel, and it does not fail a phase — but it does prevent an unqualified claim of convergence.

So: if Chrome is quarantined and the other 13 packages verify, is the Chocolatey phase *complete*? Winget's existing answer is that scope-blocked packages are deferred inventory with logged remediation, which suggests the phase can complete while the cycle declines to claim full convergence. That needs deciding explicitly rather than falling out of the implementation, and it is worth an ADR — it is hard to reverse once baked into completion claims.

## Also worth settling

- Signature composition already diverges between providers (ADR-0002 folds the expected checksum into the Chocolatey signature because `-1` carries no information). #51 deliberately duplicated Winget's counter bookkeeping rather than extracting a shared classifier. If quarantine lands too, three near-identical mechanisms exist and extraction becomes worth reconsidering — the divergence will be better understood by then.
- A quarantine must not become a silent permanent exclusion. ADR-0002's self-healing property matters here: when the maintainer refreshes the metadata the signature changes, so the quarantine should lift rather than outlive the problem.
- `choco pin` semantics differ from a winget blocking pin (prevents upgrade vs blocks install/upgrade); confirm the analogue actually holds before relying on it.

## Not urgent

Escalation already prevents the unbounded loop this came from, and stops in about four minutes with an actionable repair plan. This is a convergence-quality improvement, not a correctness fix.
notes:
DECISION SETTLED - see docs/adr/0003-deferred-inventory-qualifies-convergence.md. This issue is unblocked for implementation.

Answer to "if Chrome is quarantined and the other 13 verify, is the Chocolatey phase complete?": YES, and the cycle completes. It reports qualified convergence rather than an unqualified claim.

The question dissolved rather than needing a new rule. CONTEXT.md had framed quarantine as "distinct from deferred", which read as if they were alternatives. They are not: quarantine is the ACTION taken against the package manager, deferred inventory is the STATUS that action produces. Orthogonal. Winget already does both at once (blocking pin + deferred inventory), so this is applying an existing rule, not inventing one. CONTEXT.md has been corrected.

Ruled out by concrete scenario: "deferred blocks completion" is untenable. Microsoft Edge is permanently technology-blocked under Winget (confirmed 2026-08-18 and 2026-08-24, recurs every Edge release, see -4ik). Under that reading this machine could never complete a cycle again.

SCOPE ADDED - the code does not currently implement the glossary. Verified in the 2026-08-24 17:00 run: "Winget machine: deferred inventory - 1 install-technology blocked" at 17:00:35, then "BOOT UPDATE CYCLE COMPLETE" and a Success toast at 17:02:19-26. $deferredCount (Invoke-BootUpdateCycle.ps1:1119) exists only to reconcile the Winget exit code and reaches nothing downstream. So the truthful-convergence invariant is being violated TODAY, independently of Chocolatey. Wiring deferred inventory into the completion claim is a prerequisite for this issue, not a consequence of it, and it fixes a live bug on its own.

Qualification is carried by log wording, notification severity, and the repair plan. NOT the exit code: every caller (upd.cmd, both scheduled tasks) reads non-zero as failure, which would assert the one thing "deferred" forbids - that a phase failed.

TERM SPLIT - "deferred" was overloaded and is now two entries in CONTEXT.md. UserCompletionDeferred is a *scope deferral* (machine pass done, user pass needs user context) and already drives completion disposition via Kind='UserContext'. *Deferred inventory* is work that cannot be attempted at all and currently drives nothing. Do not let the implementation conflate them.

title: Inventory WinGet pins, unknown versions, and Store app coverage
description: Report WinGet packages excluded from upgrade because they are pinned or have unknown versions, and evaluate an opt-in Microsoft Store/UWP verification phase without overriding intentional pins.
notes:
Identified the recurring "Winget machine: deferred inventory - 1 install-technology blocked" warning.

The package is Microsoft.Edge, in machine scope. Winget transcript (2026-08-18 13:11:20 and 2026-08-24 17:00:35, both identical):
  "1 package(s) have upgrades blocked because newer versions use a different install technology than the current installation. Uninstall each package, then install the newer version."

Not intermittent. It appears exactly when Edge has a pending upgrade, so expect it once per Edge release (~monthly); it is absent between releases because there is nothing to defer.

Verified benign on 2026-08-24: edgeupdate service is Automatic (stopped = trigger-start, normal), both MicrosoftEdgeUpdateTaskMachineCore and ...MachineUA scheduled tasks are Ready, and the EdgeUpdate-registered version (151.0.4129.101) matches msedge.exe ProductVersion (151.0.4129.101). No stale registration of the kind that caused the Chocolatey/Chrome problem. Edge self-updates via EdgeUpdate; winget cannot drive it and should not.

Winget's own remedy text ("uninstall each package, then install the newer version") is actively wrong for Edge and must not be surfaced as an operator action.

Disposition to decide: this is a permanent, benign, self-resolving deferral. Options are (a) classify technology-blocked packages as benign-deferred and log at Info rather than Warn, (b) exclude Microsoft.Edge specifically, or (c) leave as-is. Note (b) is per-invocation via ExcludePatterns and would also mask genuine Edge failures, so it is the weakest option. The phase already converges either way -- this is log-noise triage, not a convergence defect.
